 International News, Latest News 

September 18, 2026




 US appeals court puts brakes on TCN deportations 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — A United States (US) federal appeals court on Friday broadly upheld a lower court ruling restricting a Trump administration policy of deporting undocumented migrants to countries that are not their own.

The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit said people facing “third-country” deportations must be given effective notice ahead of time about where they are being sent to allow them to raise concerns about potential persecution.

Congress has made it US policy not to deport people to countries where their lives would be in danger or they could be subject to torture.

READ: No start date as yet to TCN agreement — Johnson Smith

“An individual’s right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” said Judge Seth Aframe, writing for the unanimous three-judge panel.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy “would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” the judge said.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the case to the conservative-dominated Supreme Court.

Donald Trump campaigned for president promising to expel millions of undocumented migrants from the United States and has taken a number of actions aimed at speeding up deportations since returning to the White House.

The Trump administration has defended third-country deportations as necessary since the home nations of some of those who are targeted for removal sometimes refuse to accept them.

Tens of thousands of Haitians faced the prospect of leaving the United States or being deported, with the special protected status allowing them to live and work legally in the country set to expire on Aug. 3, 2026. The US Supreme Court said last month the Trump administration could end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians and some 6,000 Syrians without judicial review, although the impact of the decision could apply to migrants from many other backgrounds. (Photo: AFP) 

 International News, Latest News, Regional 

September 18, 2026




 Trump’s targeting of Haitian immigrants takes toll on US healthcare system 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — Like many Haitian healthcare workers in the United States (US), Rachelle has been forced into hiding by US President Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant policies.

“We take care of sick people. We don’t commit any crimes. So why hunt us down like animals?” the New York nurse in her 30s told AFP, speaking under a pseudonym for fear of the authorities.

After years spent caring for sick Americans, Rachelle faces deportation, like hundreds of thousands of her compatriots — which in turn is straining many American hospitals, nursing homes and healthcare facilities that rely on them.

At the end of July, the US government revoked her Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which allowed her to live and work temporarily in the United States due to dire conditions in Haiti.

Rachelle’s employer then fired her, and she has stayed home since, fearful of getting detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents if she went outside.

“I wake up every day praying that they’ve changed their minds,” she said of administration officials.

Established after the devastating 2010 earthquake, TPS status was benefiting more than 350,000 Haitians, a third of whom worked in the US healthcare sector when it was revoked, according to estimates.

That’s created “chaos” in a sector already struggling to find enough workers, and degrades patient care, said Nancy Hagans, a nurse who heads a New York City healthcare workers’ union.

Hagans said that in her facility, 21 workers were let go. In a nearby nursing home, hundreds were fired, she said.

“These workers were providing care to the most vulnerable,” she said.

In Florida, home to a large chunk of the Haitian diaspora, two home care agencies have been forced to close, said Denise Bellville, president of an association representing stakeholders in the sector.

While some caregivers continue to work undocumented in homes despite the risk of arrest, most employers have resigned themselves to layoffs, she explained.

Replacing these workers is nearly impossible.

The healthcare sector was already facing a staff shortage and relied heavily on immigrant labour to fill the lowest-paying positions, such as nursing assistants and personal care aides.

“Americans don’t choose that type of job. It’s not their focus,” Bellville said. “They can make more money doing something else”, like working in a fast-food restaurant or for Amazon.

The Trump administration has also revoked TPS for other countries such as Ethiopia, South Sudan and Yemen, and is expected to remove it soon for others like Ukraine, raising the spectre of deportation over more than a million immigrants.

All this will have repercussions for Americans, warned Bellville.

“It’s not just the employee who is sent back to their country of origin; it affects all the patients they were caring for,” she said, particularly those receiving home care who could then lose the ability to remain in their own residences.

While some healthcare facilities are trying to retain these caregivers by changing their status, the process is generally very long and expensive, and was made even more complex by the Trump administration.

Rachelle had hoped to begin this lengthy process soon when the axe fell.

“I was devastated,” recalled Rachelle, who is not considering returning to Haiti due to the unstable security situation there.

Also, Rachelle’s son, whom she raises alone, suffers from a neurodevelopmental disorder and needs specialised support that would be impossible for her to obtain otherwise.

Healthcare worker associations, industry stakeholders and local elected officials are urging Congress to reinstate protected status for Haitians.

A bill to this effect was passed in April by the House of Representatives and is now awaiting Senate approval.

“Whether they like it or not, they need us,” Rachelle said, still hoping for a positive outcome.

 Latest News, Sports 

September 18, 2026




 Brentford batter Chelsea to undo Alonso’s promising start 







LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Brentford exposed Chelsea’s defensive problems to inflict a damaging 3-0 defeat on Friday that gives Xabi Alonso plenty to ponder over a three-week international break.

After a promising start to life under the former Real Madrid coach, Chelsea have picked up just one point from their last three league games.

Goals from Jaidon Anthony, Igor Thiago and Fabio Carvalho took unbeaten Brentford above their west London neighbours and up to third in the table.

“I have this unbelievable calm around that team because I trust them. It’s nice to see it come to fruition,” said Brentford boss Keith Andrews.

Chelsea had quickly earned the reputation as the Premier League’s great entertainers under Alonso with their opening four games containing 19 goals.

But the loss of Joao Pedro to a knee injury subdued the Blues’ free-flowing attack as Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers were comfortably kept in check by the Bees.

“At the moment we are not being consistent enough to compete during the whole game,” said Alonso.

“It’s about everything. It’s about the mentality. It’s about football, tactical things that we need to keep improving that we can do much better.”

Alonso said after last weekend’s 2-2 draw against Hull, he was hoping for more “boring” games going forward.

The Spaniard sought control as he made four changes in all, handing Jordan Henderson his first Chelsea start against the 36-year-old’s former club.

Alonso got his wish during a flat first half in which neither goalkeeper was seriously tested, but Brentford were the more threatening side in the second period.

The visitors’ frailty from set-pieces led to the opening goal when Jannick Schuster rose highest to meet Mikkel Damsgaard’s corner and Anthony was left with a simple task to head into an unguarded net just after the hour mark.

Chelsea’s response was muted, and as they pushed forward in search of an equaliser, Alonso’s men were picked off on the counter-attack.

Kevin Schade should have scored the second goal himself when played clean through on Emi Martinez.

But even after the Argentine goalkeeper spread himself to save, the rebound fell kindly for Thiago to end his goal drought.

The Brazilian netted 25 times last season, earning a shock call-up to Carlo Ancelotti’s World Cup squad as a result.

Thiago has looked shorn of confidence in the early weeks of the campaign and tore off his shirt in celebration after netting for the first time in the Premier League this season.

Chelsea have conceded at least twice in all five league games under Alonso and there was further punishment to come in stoppage time.

Schade’s low cross was deflected into the path of Carvalho who fired high past Martinez to leave Andrews yelling into the night sky in delight.

Brentford, who also beat Tottenham 3-0 on the opening weekend of the season, sit behind only defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City at the top of the table.

By contrast, Chelsea were handed another reminder of the gap Alonso must bridge to make them title contenders once more.

 Trinidad man sentenced to 18 years for repeatedly sexually abusing boy 







PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) – A High Court judge in Trinidad on Friday sentenced a 48-year-old man to 18 years in prison after he was found guilty of repeatedly raping a 15-year-old boy, whom he had befriended after running away from his home more than a decade ago.

A nine-member jury had in June found Nigel Gordon Phillip guilty on two charges of buggery after the prosecution had accused him of committing the crimes during the period April to May 2015.

The court was told that the teen had left his Laventille home along the east-west corridor following an argument with his grandmother, whom he lived with, over his reluctance to join the Military-Led Academic Training (MiLAT) programme.

He went to a fast food restaurant in Port ofSpain where he met the then 38-year-old Phillip, who invited the teen to his home after hearing that he ran away and had nowhere to go. His grandmother reported him missing later that evening.

The teen said that Phillip overpowered and buggered him shortly after they arrived at his house. Phillip is reported to have kept the teen at his house for almost two months and buggered him several times. The victim claimed Phillip ordered him to clean the house and wash his clothes.

He also alleged that Phillip got a job for him at a near-by supermarket and would wait for him after he finished his shift. He claimed he was required to hand over his salary when he was paid.

The teenager, who turned 16 while at Phillip’s house, eventually escaped and made a report to the police, leading to Phillip’s arrest.

In deciding on the sentence to be imposed, Justice Nalani Singh began with a starting point of 11 years, considering also the victim’s age, his vulnerability and the circumstances in which Phillip came to exercise influence and control over him.

“That created a considerable imbalance in age, maturity, resources, and control. The prisoner’s exploitation of the position which he had assumed materially increases the seriousness of each offence,” she said.

Justice Singh said that Phillip, who worked as a security officer, Spanish tutor, and football coach, had not been charged or convicted of a criminal offence before being accused by the teen. He was also in a long-term relationship and had a 16-year-old child, both of whom he is financially responsible for.

“His previous good character, employment history, and family support justify a meaningful but measured reduction,” she said, ruling that the sentences should run consecutively and not concurrently, meaning that Phillip would serve 18 years instead of nine.

“Having considered both the individuality of the offences and their factual connection, I am satisfied that an aggregate sentence of 18 years properly reflects the prisoner’s overall criminality and is not disproportionate or excessive,” she said.

news.title: Trump administration begins building border wall in Texas’ Big Bend region
news.text: COMSTOCK, Texas: The Trump administration has started building the border wall through a west Texas section of the Big Bend region, marking the first major construction in an area of the U.S.-Mexico border where the administration's plans have met heavy opposition.The start of construction marks an important milestone in the administration's $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology as it seeks to make good on a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump to finish the wall. And it comes as Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace at which it is building the wall across the U.S.-Mexico border.Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.CBP said the first panels were erected on September 15. On a map on the agency’s website where the agency posts updates of wall construction across the entire southern border, a photo showed a crane lifting one of the 30-foot-tall steel wall panels into place while construction workers looked on.The new activity was separate from a border infrastructure project in the nearby Big Bend National Park, where the administration has temporarily suspended construction in an attempt to reach out to opponents.Activist plan to keep up their fightIn the broader Big Bend region of Texas, CBP has run up against concerted opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote region isn't a high-traffic area for illegal immigration.Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.Clara Benson, one of the founders of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition which has been fighting against CBP’s plans, said in an interview Friday that the organization had been receiving reports of trucks moving supplies into the remote area along the Rio Grande and that contractors had been clearing yards to stage supplies..But speaking from Washington, D.C. where she and others in the coalition were meeting with lawmakers, she said that the organization and others would continue to fight the wall-building plans across the region.“We will continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is. We will continue fighting to the end,” said Benson. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”Trump has vowed to complete the border wallThe news comes as the administration is speeding forward with a plan to line the entire border with a combination of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, barriers designed to stop vehicles from crossing the border, new patrol roads, and various technologies to deter and detect migrants or smugglers from crossing the border.Customs and Border Protection said it is building an average of 12 miles of barriers per week along the 2,000-mile border with Mexico and recently reached a milestone of 200 miles of new barriers built since the second Trump administration took office.The 12-miles-a-week average is double the pace that the agency's head, Rodney Scott, cited earlier this year.The agency has faced opposition from environmental groups, a small town that worries the wall will cause flooding in its area, Native Americans who say the construction is disturbing sacred sites and landowners who say the construction will infringe on their land.In Texas, much of the opposition has centered on the agency's plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state's southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world. But up and downriver outside the park, much of the land is owned by private landowners, many of whom have pushed back against the government's efforts.Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.Activists and landowners have also shown up at county meetings to push their elected officials not to cooperate with contractors hired by CBP to build the wall, and many landowners have refused to allow government officials or contractors onto their land to survey it..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: លោក Trump ប្រកាសអំពីកិច្ចព្រមព្រៀង ស្តីអំពីបញ្ហាសន្តិសុខ ជាមួយនឹងដាណឺម៉ាក
news.text:
បរទេស៖យោងតាមការចេញ ផ្សាយរបស់ RT លោកប្រធានាធិបតី Donald Trump បានប្រកាសថា សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិកនឹងគ្រប់គ្រង សន្តិសុខរបស់ Greenland ប្រកបដោយប្រសិទ្ធភាព ក្រោម

កិច្ចព្រមព្រៀង ដែលសម្រេចបានជាមួយប្រទេសដាណឺម៉ាក និងតំបន់អាកទិកដែលគ្រប់គ្រងដោយខ្លួនឯង ។

នៅក្នុងការបង្ហោះ Truth Social កាលពីថ្ងៃសុក្រ លោក Trump បាននិយាយថា កិច្ចព្រមព្រៀងនេះ នឹងផ្តល់ឱ្យសហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក នូវការគ្រប់គ្រងជាអចិន្ត្រៃយ៍លើសន្តិសុខ និងតម្រូវការផ្សេងទៀត

ទាំងអស់នៅក្នុង Greenland ដោយដោះស្រាយទាំងស្រុងនូវរាល់កង្វល់ ជាច្រើនរបស់សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក ។

លោកបានបន្ថែមថា៖តាមការណែនាំរបស់ខ្ញុំ យើងបានធ្វើការជាមួយតំណាង នៃប្រទេសដាណឺម៉ាក និងហ្គ្រីនឡែន ដើម្បីធានាថាសហរដ្ឋអាមេរិកនឹងមានសមត្ថភាពពេញលេញដើម្បីធ្វើអ្វីដែលចាំបាច់នៅ

ក្នុងហ្គ្រីនលែន ដើម្បីធានា និងការពារសន្តិសុខ នៃហ្គ្រីនឡែន និងសហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក។

លើសពីនេះទៅទៀត ចាប់ពីពេលនេះតទៅ គ្មានសត្រូវរបស់សហរដ្ឋអាមេរិក អាចមានមូលដ្ឋាននៅ Greenland មានវត្តមានយោធានៅ Greenland ឬធ្វើការវិនិយោគដ៏រសើបនៅក្នុង Greenland

នោះទេដោយគ្មានការយល់ព្រមជាលាយលក្ខណ៍អក្សររបស់យើងឡើយ។

គួរឲ្យដឹងដែរថាការប្រកាសរបស់លោក Trump ធ្វើឡើងស្របពេលជាមួយ នឹងកិច្ចប្រជុំមន្ត្រីយោធាកំពូល របស់ណាតូនៅទីក្រុង Copenhagen ជាកន្លែងដែលប្រធានការពារជាតិចំនួន៣២ នាក់របស់សម្ព័ន្ធភាព

បានប្រមូលផ្តុំគ្នាដើម្បីពិភាក្សាអំពីការពង្រឹងការទប់ស្កាត់ និងការការពាររួម៕

news.title: Protesters surround Kennedy Centre over Trump demolition fears
news.text:
Thousands of people joined outside the John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts on Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump’s plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organisations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution.
The crowd streamed in from the nearest subway stop, crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carrying signs, as they joined in “Hands Around the Kennedy Centre”. Many carried signs, wore costumes and booed when the president was mentioned during the programme.
Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people were willing to fight to keep Trump’s plans for the building at bay.
One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Centre has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favourites onto its governing board.
Late last year, he had his name placed on the centre. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

The Kennedy Centre board, which is aligned with the president, voted on Tuesday to close the centre indefinitely for repairs hours after US District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked its plans to return Trump’s name to the building.
On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Centre to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it.
Raleigh said he, like others, was concerned that Trump could take the step without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.”
Raleigh said the Kennedy Centre was more in the public eye than the East Wing was. He added he did not believe the president fully understood why people were so upset “but that’s our job, right? This may be the line that no one expected but this is where the line is going to be”.
Importance of arts
Protesters talked about the importance of the centre as the pinnacle of the nation’s performing arts world.
Bud Wilkinson, a local member of the arts community, set up a chalkboard with Trump’s name written on it hundreds of times. Protesters flocked to him to erase the names and replace them with hearts.
“The Kennedy Centre is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” Wilkinson said. “This is not just about putting the president’s name on the Kennedy Centre. It’s about censoring the performances and the programming. That’s what started all this. So that’s what the nitty-gritty really is about. So I want to replace all of this with love. That’s why there’s a heart.”
Alina Baciu talked about the opportunities and relationships that students at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts had with the centre and how those relationships might be impacted by what was going on.
Her daughter had numerous opportunities to take advantage of all the centre had to offer as a student at Duke Ellington, she said. “They borrowed the beautiful costumes and the beautiful dresses from the Washington National Opera for their performances at Duke Ellington,” she said. They also performed on the centre’s Millennium Stage.
“All of those things have gone away because of this craziness. And it just hurts my heart.”

Laura Steinberg, a volunteer for the last 10 years, said the loss of performances has already been heart-wrenching.
“This reminds me of that picture from Tiananmen Square, where that young man stood in front of the tank,” she said of the throngs present. “This was my visceral response to this. I’ll stand in front of the wrecking ball if it’s going to come to that. My guess is many of these people would come down because we saw what he did to the East Wing. Nobody thought he would actually do it. So I think the shock has mobilised people.”
Friday’s event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington where filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continued to push for the president’s vanity projects.
The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump’s triumphal arch, and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the US Institute of Peace.
Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the centre, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it.
“We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it,” he said. “I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Centre.”

news.title: Thousands join protest outside Kennedy Center, expressing concern that Trump might tear it down
news.text: WASHINGTON: Thousands of people joined outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump's plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organizations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution.The crowd streamed in from the nearest subway stop, crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carrying signs, as they joined in “Hands Around the Kennedy Center.” At one point some held hands and formed a human chain around the center.Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people are willing to fight to keep Trump's plans for the building at bay.One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Center has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favorites onto its governing board. Late last year, he had his named placed on the center. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed.The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked their plans to return Trump’s name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it.Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned that Trump could take the step without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.”Raleigh said the Kennedy Center is more in the public eye than the East Wing was. He added he doesn’t believe the president fully understands why people are so upset “but that’s our job right? This may be the line that no one expected but this is where the line is going to be.”.A landmark of the performing arts has gone silentProtesters talked about the importance of the center as the pinnacle of the nation's performing arts world.Bud Wilkinson, a local member of the arts community, set up a chalkboard with Trump's name written on it hundreds of times. Protesters flocked to him to erase the names and replace them with hearts.“The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” Wilkinson said. “This is not just about putting the president’s name on the Kennedy Center. It’s about censoring the performances and the programming. That’s what started all this. So that’s what the nitty-gritty really is about this. So I want to replace all of this with love. That’s why there’s a heart.”Alina Baciu talked about the opportunities and relationships that students at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts have with the center and how those relationships might be impacted by what's going on.Her daughter had numerous opportunities to take advantage of all the center had to offer as a student at Duke Ellington, she said. “I mean, they borrowed the beautiful costumes and the beautiful dresses from the Washington National Opera for their performances at Duke Ellington,” she said. They also performed on the center's Millennium Stage."All of those things have gone away because of this craziness. And it just hurts my heart,” Baciu said.Laura Steinberg, a volunteer for the last 10 years, said the loss of performances has already been heart- wrenching. “This reminds me of that picture from Tiananmen Square, where that young man stood in front of the tank,” she said of the throngs present. “This was my visceral response to this. I’ll stand in front of the wrecking ball if it’s going to come to that. My guess is many of these people would come down because we saw what he did to the East Wing. Nobody thought he would actually do it. So I think the shock has mobilized people.”.Friday's event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington where filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continues pushing for the president’s vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump's triumphal arch and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the U.S. Institute of Peace.Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the center, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it.“We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it," he said. "I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognized as having saved the Kennedy Center.”.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

 Father clueless if daughter was intimate with Pastor Kevin Smith 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — The father of Taneka Gardner, the 39-year-old woman who had her throat slashed on October 17, 2021, at the Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James, told a defence attorney on Thursday during cross-examination that he had no knowledge of his daughter being in a romantic relationship with the late pastor of the church, Dr Kevin Smith.

The murder trial of Andre Ruddock, the man accused of killing Gardner, got underway in the Home Circuit Court in Kingston on Thursday after a seven-member jury was empanelled on Wednesday.

Ruddock, under instructions from Smith, allegedly cut Gardner’s throat during what is widely believed to be a sacrificial killing.

Attorney-at-law Venice Brown, who along with Anthony Williams is representing Ruddock, appeared to have known something about a romantic relationship between Smith and Gardner, as the few questions she posed to the witness were mainly centred on that topic.

Brown asked the father if his daughter was involved romantically with Smith and he responded, “I don’t know about that one.

Brown right after suggested to the father that his daughter was in a romantic relationship with the pastor, however, trial Judge Leighton Pusey pointed out to her that the witness already indicated that he knew nothing about the alleged romance and prompted her to move on to the next question.

The next question to the father was if his daughter had any known medical conditions before she died.

“No, madam,” the father said to the attorney, who had no further questions.

During examination-in-chief, prosecutor LaToya Bernard asked the father a series of questions to establish for the seven jurors that he actually buried his daughter and that she was in fact dead.

The father shared that he received a call on October 18, the day after the incident, which prompted him to go to the church in Albion.

“I just went there because I heard what happened. I saw the police and the yellow tape. A lot of police and yellow tape, caution tape. I saw the tape blocking the entrance to the church. No madam, I didn’t go over to the church when I saw the caution tape,” he said.

He explained that he then proceeded to a location he referred to as Mango Walk, where his cousin resided. He explained that both of them went to the Freeport Police Station where he spoke to a detective inspector.

“I left for the Delapenha Funeral Home in Montego Bay, St James, to see the body because they said the body was there. They took out the body and showed it to me. It was Taneka Gardner, my daughter. I saw a slash on her throat. Workers from Delapenha were there with me. My cousin didn’t come inside.

“On November 19, 2021, I was called to come to St Catherine at Archer’s Funeral Home in Spanish Town. When I got there I was early so I waited until they opened. I went inside and a policeman spoke to me and took me to a room where the doctor was going to perform the autopsy. Taneka Gardner’s body was on a table and I was asked to identify her and I identified her as Taneka Gardner to the doctor as well as the police,” he said, explaining that he last spoke to his daughter about four days before she was killed.

After Gardner’s father left the witness stand, Corey James, the second witness, took up his position to give the jurors his chilling account of what occurred at the church on that fateful day in 2021.

“>He confirmed knowing Ruddock — the accused — very well as both of them had been attending the church together since 2014.

James, who is a livestock farmer, confirmed that Smith was the head of the church and that other members including himself and Ruddock were given various roles and functions.

He shared that while Ruddock was a security guard and Smith’s bodyguard, he on the other hand was given the role of getting Smith dressed and shaving his head.

“I helped Dr Smith get dressed before services,” he told the court.

James said that on the day of the incident, there was not supposed to be any service at the church because the day before, on Saturday, October 16, 2021, there was a “special ceremony”.

So, on the Sunday while he was cooking and resting, he had no intentions of going to church. However, his wife ran upstairs to him and told him something. He got out of bed and started to get ready to head down to the church. Asked by prosecutor Bernard why he, his wife and others got ready for church, James explained that Pastor Smith made a Facebook post where he informed his congregants of a flood and instructed them to come to him for safe haven.

“After she spoke with me we got ready, my wife, myself, our daughter and one of her friends, her friend’s mother and a nephew,” he said.

“Dr Smith made a post on Facebook. It was not his first time. He would post on his timeline on Facebook. Dr Smith made a post that a flood was coming. I am not sure what flood it was, but that was what he said, and we should come to the church for a safe haven. Yes, I did believe that a flood was coming, and I got ready and went to the church. When I reached the church it was between 1:00 pm and 3:00 pm. My family and friends travelled with me.

“When I got there, there were other individuals there. I was in yellow shorts, a blue hoodie, and I had a white sheet covering myself. Dr Smith said we should all cover ourselves with a white sheet. Everyone who travelled with me had a white sheet. When I got to the church, I saw others covered in white sheet. The covering up with the sheet was something new that started on the 16th, the day before at the special ceremony.

“I went on the boardwalk and was going inside the building. Dr Smith was at the top of the step at the main entrance of the building. Yes, I spoke with Dr Kevin Smith, and he spoke to me. I entered the building and sat down on the ground. He told us all to sit on the ground, cover ourselves with the sheets and not look in his face. Around 12 individuals [were in the building]. Mr Michael Brown, my wife’s cousin, was also at the church. Dr Smith started speaking. We started throwing food stuff outside. We threw away sanitary napkins, tissue and other stuff out the front of the building. 

Because of COVID-19, Dr Smith was telling us the world was coming to an end,” James said, pointing out that the pastor was frequently telling them to take their money out of the bank.

He said Smith told them to throw out the food and other stuff because they were from Babylon.

While James and others threw out the items, he explained that a bottle fell from a table and broke on the ground inside the church.

He told the court that Smith informed them that those who were on the opposite side of the bottle would have to die in order for them to enter into the Kingdom.

“He said he got a revelation. I was on the opposite side, and Dr Smith said to me that in order for me to come over on the other side, my throat has to be cut. I was confused when he mentioned that to me. I spoke to Dr Smith, and he said I was a demon and that I should come out of the sanctuary. After I was told my throat would be cut, Kevaughn Plummer approached me with a knife, and he was trying to put the knife under my throat. I rest my finger under my neck to push away the knife. The knife was right under my chin. Dr Smith said I should get out.”

He said that when he turned around to walk outside, he felt someone stab him in the back, causing him to run out on the pavement.

“I felt like something was running down in my back. I wiped my back, and when I looked, I saw blood. Mr Smith was standing at the entrance of the door when I turned around. He said something to me. I spoke to Andre Ruddock and asked him if he could tie the white cloth around my back. He did not tie it, but Aldeane Campbell tied it for me. There were a lot of people outside the fence on the road, including my mom, sister, nephew and other people I would call friends. They wanted to come on the compound. The gate was closed, so they weren’t able to come over.”

The witness said he remained at the church because his wife and his daughter were still inside.

While on the outside of the church building, James said he could hear things being smashed and broken on the inside.

“It was still bright, so it was maybe around after 3:00 pm. Persons were shouting on the outside, ‘it’s Israel God, Israel King’. This was on the outside of the fence on the roadside. He shared that Smith took out a piece of paper with names on it. Among the names on the list were Taneka Gardner.

He appointed two archangels, Ruddock and another man and gave them two knives. He then instructed them to go to the church gate and not let anybody else in unless their names were called.

When Gardner was called, she entered and signed 999 beside her name on the paper. She was given instructions, including to kneel down.

“When Kevin Smith called Taneka Gardner’s name, Andrew Ruddock and Kayon Ramsey opened the gate and let her in. The people on the outside of the gate, I could see them over the picket fence. When Taneka Gardner was allowed to come on the inside, she was covered in the white garment. White cloth was tied around her head. I could see her face when she came in. Her head was covered as well. She had a suitcase in her hand, a mini suitcase. She came in with it and Kevin Smith asked her where she was going with that bag. One of the young men took it from her and went back to the gate with it.

“Kevin Smith said, ‘Taneka Gardner, your blood is not clean’. He was speaking very loudly. He continued to speak to her. He asked her, ‘do you believe that I am God? Do you believe I can heal you?’ She said Yes. He went further and he said, do you believe that if you die I can bring you back to life? She shouted on the top of her voice and said yes. Dr Smith gave a command. He said, ‘Archangel, cut her throat.’ He appointed Kayon Ramsey and Andre Ruddock as Archangel Gabriel and Michael.

“I was looking directly in the direction of Andre Ruddock. I watched Andre use his elbow to nudge Kayon Ramsey, but Kayon did not move. Andre Ruddock ran off from the gate and ran towards Taneka Gardner. Miss Taneka Gardner was kneeling down, and Andre Ruddock put the knife at her throat, and he was rubbing her throat with the knife. I just saw her foot kicking, and I could hear a gargling sound, like the blood was rushing down her windpipe as if she had fluid in her mouth, like when you put water in your mouth and gargle. He was rubbing the knife at her throat for about a minute before he brought her down to the ground. Mr Smith said to him to cut her head right off. While Andre Ruddock was cutting her throat, a cow was coming down from up the top,” he said, telling the court that it was at that time Smith switched focus from Gardner and told Ruddock and Ramsey to kill the cow.

The witness explained that Ruddock then got up from where Gardner was, while Ramsey chased down the cow.

“Taneka Gardner was just lying there. You could see the white sheet with what appeared to be blood and it was also on the sheet that Andre Ruddock had on,” he said.

news.title: US Democrats fight over party's future as Trump targets 'communists'
news.text:
Melat Kiros knows she doesn't fit the mould of a typical member of the US Congress.

The Ethiopian-born Democratic Socialist is on track to become the first gen Z woman to enter Congress, hoping to ride a wave of anti-establishment sentiment on the American left.

"Americans right now are reckoning with the fact that things have been broken for quite a while," she told the ABC.

"We've found that the mainstream ideas coming out of both parties have failed."

Kiros, 29, is vying for a safe Democratic seat in Denver, Colorado, after winning a primary election to bump the incumbent of nearly three decades from the Democrats' ticket.

Before her run in politics, she was fired from her job as a corporate lawyer.

In 2023, she wrote an open letter criticising the stance numerous US law firms, including her own, took in support of Israel after the Hamas terrorist attacks.

In her post, she condemned antisemitism, calling it "the longest hatred", but argued it should not be conflated "with the geopolitical question of Israel's legitimacy".

She was asked to take it down and refused.

Her criticism of the Israeli government over the Gaza war now forms a key part of her campaign.

Like many Democratic Socialists, she is calling for a total arms embargo on the country: a position that has angered "moderate" elements of the party and contributed to their widening split with "progressives".

"Our tax dollars are actively participating in this," Kiros said of Israel's bombardment of Gaza.

 "We have the ability to end the violence right now if only we just end our tax dollars that are being sent there."

She also wants to make dramatic cuts to defence spending and instead put money towards universal healthcare, childcare and expanding public housing.

"This notion that what we're calling for is extreme is detached from reality [when] all these developed nations that are our peers already have a lot of these programs."

Factional fight

Kiros is one of several candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which have had success in recent Democrat primary races ahead of the midterm elections.

The organisation, whose policies include higher taxes on the wealthy and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, is proving popular on the left.

A recent CBS-YouGov poll found 71 per cent of participants who identified as liberal voters held favourable views on socialism.

But the rise of the progressive left has sparked a civil war within the Democratic Party as it fights over its future direction.

Centrist Democrat group Third Way has launched a $US15 million ($21 million) campaign to discredit democratic socialism within the party.

"The fight is important to have," said Third Party co-founder Jim Kessler, a former staffer to Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer.

"It's important to push the Democratic Party back to the centre because we cannot win with a far-left candidate in a general election.

"We are a centre-right nation, and there are more conservatives in America than there are liberals … so the math is such that we just have to win a super-majority of moderates.

"Republicans don't have to."

While socialism polls favourably among liberal voters, a New York Times/Siena poll this month found about half of Americans view it unfavourably.

Most DSA-backed candidates who won their primaries are in safe Democratic seats, and Kessler said moderate candidates have seen success in swing seats where they are more appealing to independent or disillusioned Republican voters.

"A lot of the solutions on the far left are slogans; they're not really solutions," he said.

"There needs to be flesh on the bones, and they don't want to put the flesh on the bones because it opens them up to criticism."

Trump's midterms attacks

But Kiros argues the US and the world are in precarious times and cannot afford another "do nothing Democratic administration".

"We have no choice but to fight for bold solutions, or else this democracy will not survive," she said.

"Voters are desperately looking for anybody or any group that's actually offering ideas and solutions that can meet this moment right now.

"I think Democratic Socialists are the only ones that have done that in a meaningful way and that's why we're winning."

Republican President Donald Trump has leapt at the opportunity to attack the rising left faction of the Democrats.

"They call themselves Democratic socialist, but actually they're communists," he told the Republican midterm convention earlier this month.

He and other Republicans hope to paint them as a danger to the economy and country ahead of the November midterms, where Republicans risk losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

"If they win, the greatest legislative body in history will, for the first time ever, be controlled by a communist caucus," Trump said.

But in progressive Denver, and cities across the US, the movement is spreading.

Craig Skinner joined the local branch after watching Zohran Mamdani win the New York City mayoral election.

He felt inspired to "get off the couch" and "be part of something", so he joined Kiros's campaign and started volunteering.

"Our membership has nearly doubled since the beginning of the Melat campaign," he said.

Skinner argues Trump once made similar promises to the American people about lowering the cost of living and rooting out establishment politics, but failed to deliver.

"When you go to so many doors and hear so many people excited about what Denver DSA stands for and what Melat stands for, it's hard to say that's radical," Skinner said.

"It's policy that changes the way that people can interact with the economy, whether that's publicly financed campaigns or giving everybody healthcare.

"We're already paying so many taxes and [yet] some people aren't being taxed enough: the millionaires, the billionaires and the corporations in this country.

"That is a message that people get behind when you tell them."
news.summary: The rise of the progressive left has sparked a civil war among US Democrats as the party fights over its future direction ahead of November's midterms battle with Donald Trump's Republicans.

news.title: Trump claims permanent US security role in Greenland under new Denmark deal
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington “permanent control” over Greenland’s security, including measures aimed at preventing Russia and China from establishing military or commercial footholds in the strategically important Arctic territory.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needs control of Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.

Trump said the agreement would give the United States permanent control over “security, and all other needs” in Greenland and would allow Washington to immediately begin developing a larger military presence there.

“From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

The 80-year-old president described the agreement as an “‘Infinite Life’ Agreement” with “no end.”

The office of Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the three governments would sign the agreement next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

However, Denmark said parliamentary action would still be required in Denmark and Greenland before the agreement could take effect.

Frederiksen said the agreement recognized “the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Greenland and Denmark and upheld their right to self-determination.

“I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” she said, adding that it was good for NATO and Europe.

Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the emerging agreement strengthened the territory’s security and recognized “Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation.”

Blocking Russia and China

A State Department official said the agreement would prohibit non-NATO bases in Greenland and establish mechanisms to prevent Russia and China from deploying troops or establishing bases or making sensitive investments there.

“This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” the official said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the announcement as a “historic deal” and a “huge win” for the United States.

“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Rubio said, adding that the agreement “permanently and completely addresses” US national security concerns in Greenland.

Trump has repeatedly cited increased Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic as a reason Washington needs greater control over Greenland, whose location between North America and Europe gives it major strategic importance. Its mineral resources have also increased its geopolitical significance.

Details remain unclear

Trump gave few details about how the agreement would operate, and it was not immediately clear whether it was linked to or substantially different from an understanding he announced with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.

Several media outlets have reported that Washington wants to establish three additional military bases in southern Greenland, alongside the US base at Pituffik in the north.

A 1951 US-Danish defense agreement, updated in 2004, already permits Washington to increase troop deployments and military installations on Greenland, provided it notifies Denmark and Greenland in advance.

Despite their opposition to Trump’s demands for control of Greenland, Danish officials have repeatedly said they were prepared to work with Washington to expand the US military presence and strengthen American commercial interests on the island.

NATO tensions

Trump’s push for Greenland has nevertheless strained relations with Denmark and other European allies.

After returning to office, Trump called on Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States and repeatedly refused to rule out using military force to take the territory, which has about 57,000 inhabitants and is an autonomous part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly said Greenland is not for sale and objected to reports of US intelligence-gathering activities on the island. Russia and much of Europe have also opposed the US campaign for greater control of the territory.

The confrontation rattled NATO and was seen in Denmark and other European capitals as a challenge to their sovereignty, said Imran Bayoumi, an associate director at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.

“I think Americans really underestimate how damaging it was for the image of the United States in Europe,” he said. “I think Greenlanders, Danes, Europeans saw this as a real attack on their sovereignty, and it’s going to take a lot of work to repair.”

Tensions have eased somewhat since the height of the dispute. In an apparent effort to address Washington’s security concerns, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Denmark’s Frederiksen said earlier this week that she was “optimistic” that discussions with Washington and Greenland, which had continued since January, could resolve the dispute.

Trump said Friday that the United States looked forward to working with Denmark and Greenland toward “a magnificent future” involving the “large, and highly strategic” territory, adding: “We will be very protective of it.”

 10 things only a Westwood High girl would know 







Westwood High School is known for producing talented, well-educated and poised young ladies. The institution, which has been in existence for more than a century, can credit much of this to its vibrant culture and traditions. 

Observer Online spoke to a number of the Stewart Town, Trelawny-based school’s alumni to find out some of the things that every Westwood girl would know.

1. Jippi Jappa hat and wearing all white

Westwood High is one of the few schools in Jamaica where students wear hats as part of their uniform. The tradition, which has its roots in English school customs, has been passed down and retained by the institution over the years. The Jippi Jappa hat, also known as a Panama hat, is worn by the young ladies along with their uniforms. Students are not permitted to wear the hat past the principal’s building.

Students are also expected to have a set of white clothing outside of their regular uniform. This is worn on occasions when they are not required to be in uniform, except on Friday evenings and Saturdays.

2. The Jacaranda tree

The Jacaranda tree was one of the familiar landmarks on the Westwood campus and a popular meeting spot for students during break time. The ladies gathered beneath the tree to catch up with friends, relax and enjoy each other’s company. With its vibrant purple blooms and towering structure, the tree provided both a scenic and comfortable setting. Unfortunately, the tree has been cut down, but it remains a memorable part of the Westwood experience.

3. Observing silence

Silence is a familiar part of life at Westwood. Students are expected to observe silence during prep or study time, meal times and intervals. For many old girls, learning when to talk and when to remain quiet was simply part of the discipline and routine of school life.

4. Sarcasm and lapsing

Westwood ladies are known for their quick wit and, according to old girls, their ability to dish out a healthy dose of sarcasm. They also participate in what is known as “lapsing”. This is when a word is mispronounced and other students repeat the word or phrase, often drawing attention to the mistake. For Westwood girls, it is all part of the banter and camaraderie that develop among students.

5. Knife and fork

Table manners are a big part of the meal-time experience at Westwood. Students are expected to eat their meals using a knife and fork and to follow proper dining etiquette. This includes knowing how to conduct themselves at the table and, in some cases, asking permission before doing things such as chewing bones at the table. For many students, these lessons extended beyond the dining hall and became part of the poise and etiquette associated with being a Westwood girl.

6. Day girls and boarders

Westwood is one of the few schools in Jamaica that offers a boarding option for students. Those who live on the school compound are referred to as boarders, while students who travel to school are called ‘day girls’. 

7. Walking to church

Boarders are expected to walk to church on Sundays. The girls are divided based on denomination and walk together to their respective churches. For many boarders, the walk to church is a familiar part of the Westwood boarding experience.

8. Out-of-bounds areas

The ladies of Westwood know that there are certain areas of the school that they are not allowed to enter. These include the teachers’ steps and staff rooms. Students are expected to know and respect these boundaries, with venturing into out-of-bounds areas likely to result in disciplinary action.

 9. Students not allowed in stores without parental supervision

If a young lady wanted to enter a store while wearing her uniform, she had to be accompanied by a parent. If she entered a store without a parent and misbehaved, any report made to the school could result in her being reprimanded when she returned. The rule meant that students were expected to remember that their behaviour while wearing the Westwood uniform reflected on the school.

10. Silence as punishment

Silence was also used as a form of punishment at Westwood. Students who misbehave could be required to observe silence. The punishment was intended to give students time to settle down, reflect on their behaviour and regain their composure.

– Carlysia Ramdeen

news.title: Trump claims Don Jr. is paying back Putin-tied Russian oligarch for lavish wedding
news.text:
President Donald Trump has claimed that his eldest son is paying back Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev for his lavish Bahamas wedding party. 

Kremlev, the head of the scandal-ridden International Boxing Association, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on expenses incurred at Donald Trump Jr.’s multi-day party on two private islands in May to celebrate his marriage to socialite Bettina Anderson, according to a ProPublica report published Monday. 

The report sparked corruption and national security concerns, with Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, writing on X, “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”

Trump, who has disputed any personal ties with Kremlev and did not attend his son’s wedding, told reporters that Kremlev’s gift was “totally allowed,” but that his son paid the oligarch back.

“Was it appropriate for your son to accept a gift — a payment for some of his wedding festivities?” one reporter asked Trump in the Oval Office Friday. 

“It's totally allowed and a lot of people have parties,” Trump replied. “But as I understand it, he paid him back.”

“A person that he knows, I guess a friend of his, gave him a wedding party — that’s very common. I’ve heard of many people giving wedding parties,” the president continued. “I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people.”

Kremlev reportedly paid to rent one of the private islands where the Trump family and their friends partied, which ProPublica said could cost about $100,000 a night, and other expenses such as a fireworks display with an estimated price tag of about $70,000. 

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told ProPublica Kremlev was a “personal friend of Don” and that the two met through a mutual friend in the hunting community. The spokesperson added that Kremlev is “not someone [Trump Jr.] has a business relationship with.”

Bettina also spoke out following the report that Kremlev bankrolled their wedding festivities. 

She said that she wed Trump Jr. at an inmate ceremony with only family members in attendance and called the party “a fun weekend with friends.”

“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” Bettina wrote in a joint statement with Trump Jr. on her Instagram earlier this week. 

“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from,” the statement continued. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.”

Along with the statement, Bettina shared some photos, including one of herself and Trump Jr. dressed in all white on a beach as fireworks illuminated the night sky. There were also pictures of dancers dressed as sailors, a man doing a card trick and a DJ getting lost in the music. 

Kremlev, who reportedly attended the Bahamas party, “has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances,” his press office told ProPublica. 

Representative Garcia, meanwhile, has sent a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles asking for information regarding any ties between Trump Jr. and Kremlev. 

“As the son of President Donald Trump and the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter. 

Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked by a reporter in the White House Rose Garden earlier this week whether he would investigate the matter, to which he said, “Am I investigating what?”

“The president doesn't know who this person is. I think other members of the family don't know who this person is. The president's son has said he's a very close friend and that he accepted a gift in the weekend of his wedding.”
news.summary: Umar Kremlev reportedly spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the multi-day event filled with fireworks and dancers in sailor caps
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Trump signs bill allowing 100% tariffs on India, other countries for buying Russian oil
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump on Friday gave his assent to a legislation that allows him to impose tariffs of up to 100% on India and other countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.

The signing of the bill into law does not automatically trigger the tariffs.

The law states that the tariffs could apply to the five countries that imported the largest volumes of Russian crude oil or natural gas in the 12 months before the law takes effect, if they knowingly continue buying Russian crude oil 30 days after the law is enacted.

Washington has for long claimed that the purchase of Russian energy has been fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine that began in February 2022.

The bill was passed by the House of Representatives on Wednesday. The Senate had cleared it on August 7. The law is named after late Republican legislator Lindsey Graham, who had spearheaded it before he died in July.

The tariffs could also target any of the five countries identified as helping Russia evade oil-related sanctions.

However, countries that have significantly reduced their imports of Russian natural gas, or whose Russian gas imports account for less than 15% of Russia’s gas exports, would be exempt.

After the House passed the bill, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said on Thursday that New Delhi is committed to ensuring energy security for its people. “It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics,” it said.

The external affairs ministry also said that during discussions with US interlocutors, the potential implications of the matter on the bilateral relationship and the international energy market “have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side”.

“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry said. “Government will work closely with Indian trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of these developments.”

India’s Russian oil imports

The legislation comes as India has increased its purchases of Russian oil this year, while New Delhi and Washington negotiate a preliminary trade deal. India’s import of Russian oil rose to an 11-month high in April, following the US and Israel’s war on Iran.

Before this, India had reduced its purchases of Russian oil, which fell to a 38-month low in December.

Over the past year, there have been diplomatic tensions between Washington and New Delhi over India’s continued purchases of Russian crude.

The Trump administration had in August 2025 imposed a 25% punitive levy on India for buying oil from Russia amid the Ukraine war. This had taken the combined US tariff rate to 50%.

In January, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed that India had stopped buying Russian oil after Trump imposed the punitive tariff.

In February, after New Delhi and Washington agreed to an interim trade deal, Trump removed the additional 25% punitive levy linked to the purchase of Russian oil.

The US Treasury had later paused global sanctions on Russian oil shipments that were already in transit before March 11, amid supply disruptions caused by war in West Asia.

Edited by Nachiket Deuskar.
news.summary: After the US Congress passed the bill, India said it will continue to ensure energy security for its people ‘through diversified sourcing’.

news.title: Trump will be at the airport to greet Xi when China’s leader arrives for his US state visit
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The first state visit by the leader of China in more than a decade takes place next week when President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for high-stakes talks — and a little schmoozing — at the White House with President Donald Trump.

When Xi’s plan lands at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington on Wednesday, Trump will be there to welcome Xi for the state visit, senior administration officials told reporters. That’s unusual -- Trump typically meets foreign leaders at the White House.

The heart of the visit comes Thursday when Trump and first lady Melania Trump welcome Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at an arrival ceremony held indoors on the State Floor of the White House. Trump and Xi will also participate in a review of troops in the Rose Garden before they retreat behind closed doors for their talks.

The first lady and Peng Liyuan will hold a separate engagement while their spouses get down to business. Details were not released during a call the officials held Friday to brief reporters on Xi’s visit.

Xi and his wife will also be the guests of honor Thursday as Trump and the first lady host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the East Room. Trump described the dinner as an event everyone wants to attend. Both leaders will deliver remarks.

“Thousands of people would love to be at that dinner,” Trump told reporters Friday in the Oval Office. He appeared to lament that the 1,000-person ballroom he is adding onto the White House will not be available for the soiree because it is still under construction. “This is a very tough ticket for me.”

“I’ve told a lot of very good friends of mine, ‘you just can’t come,’” Trump said.

White House shares some names on the state dinner guest list

But some of the Republican president’s tech industry friends have been invited.

Among the executives scheduled to attend the state dinner are Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai of Google and Michael Dell, the CEO of Dell Technologies, the White House said.

Also on the guest list are Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup, and Tim Cook, who recently stepped down as the CEO of Apple.

Next Friday, Xi and Peng Liyuan are scheduled to return to the White House for a private tea with the Trumps, who will then take them on a tour of the National Archives, the home of some of the United States’ most important founding documents as the nation celebrates its 250th anniversary.

Xi will head for Joint Base Andrews after the tour.

Tariffs, artificial intelligence, rare earths on the agenda

As for other substantive parts of the visit, U.S. officials said Washington and Beijing may be ready to ease some tariffs on some nonstrategic goods.

Discussing the visit during a call with reporters, senior U.S. officials said such a move might affect a narrow band of goods that would advantage both sides. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House, did not elaborate.

But they said they did not expect the United States would be ready to ease export controls to allow for a greater flow of rare earth minerals, critical components in a wide range of products, into the global market.

The officials said China maintaining an acceptable flow of such minerals would be discussed, but there was unlikely to be an exchange involving reduced U.S. export controls.

Separately, Treasury Secretary Bessent will meet over the weekend in New York with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to discuss a range of economic issues, according to a person familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the details publicly.

Artificial intelligence will be a focus of the talks, the person said.

Also on the agenda will be China’s stockpiles of rare earth minerals, essential to everything from smartphones to fighter jets. Beijing has used its near-monopoly on the minerals to bring the United States to the negotiating table in a trade war started by Trump’s tariffs and other sanctions on China. The talks might continue at the working level into Monday, the person said.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will join Bessent on Sunday for the meeting with He, Greer’s office announced Friday evening.

Trump visited China in May, as well as in his first term, for talks with Xi, who rolled out the red carpet for his American counterpart.

Xi was last in the United States for a state visit in September 2015 during the administration of Democrat Barack Obama.
news.summary: President Xi Jinping’s visit marks the first Chinese state visit to the US in over a decade. President Trump plans to welcome him at the airport before high-stakes talks and a state dinner at the White House.

news.title: Thousands join protest outside Kennedy Center, expressing concern that Trump might tear it down
news.text:
Thousands of people joined outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump's plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organizations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution.

The crowd streamed in from the nearest subway stop, crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carrying signs, as they joined in “Hands Around the Kennedy Center.” Many carried signs, wore costumes and booed when the president was mentioned during the program.

Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people are willing to fight to keep Trump's plans for the building at bay.

One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Center has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favorites onto its governing board. Late last year, he had his named placed on the center. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed. 

The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked their plans to return Trump’s name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it. 

Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned that Trump could take the step without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.”

Raleigh said the Kennedy Center is more in the public eye than the East Wing was. He added he doesn’t believe the president fully understands why people are so upset “but that’s our job right? This may be the line that no one expected but this is where the line is going to be.”

 A landmark of the preforming arts has gone silent 

Protesters talked about the importance of the center as the pinnacle of the nation's performing arts world. 

Bud Wilkinson, a local member of the arts community, set up a chalkboard with Trump's name written on it hundreds of times. Protesters flocked to him to erase the names and replace them with hearts.

“The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” Wilkinson said. “This is not just about putting the president’s name on the Kennedy Center. It’s about censoring the performances and the programming. That’s what started all this. So that’s what the nitty-gritty really is about this. So I want to replace all of this with love. That’s why there’s a heart.”

Alina Baciu talked about the opportunities and relationships that students at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts have with the center and how those relationships might be impacted by what's going on.

Her daughter had numerous opportunities to take advantage of all the center had to offer as a student at Duke Ellington, she said. “I mean, they borrowed the beautiful costumes and the beautiful dresses from the Washington National Opera for their performances at Duke Ellington,” she said. They also performed on the center's Millennium Stage.

"All of those things have gone away because of this craziness. And it just hurts my heart,” Baciu said.

Laura Steinberg, a volunteer for the last 10 years, said the loss of performances has already been heart- wrenching. “This reminds me of that picture from Tiananmen Square, where that young man stood in front of the tank,” she said of the throngs present. “This was my visceral response to this. I’ll stand in front of the wrecking ball if it’s going to come to that. My guess is many of these people would come down because we saw what he did to the East Wing. Nobody thought he would actually do it. So I think the shock has mobilized people.”

Friday's event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington where filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continues pushing for the president’s vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump's triumphal arch and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the U.S. Institute of Peace.

Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the center, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it.

“We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it," he said. "I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognized as having saved the Kennedy Center.”
news.summary: Thousands of people have come to protest outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts
news.author: Gary Fields

news.title: CENTCOM puts price tag on Iran war
news.text:
The war with Iran has cost the US $43.6 billion, with nearly two-thirds of the bill going toward replenishing depleted munitions stockpiles, according to US Central Command (CENTCOM) figures sent to lawmakers and shared with the media on Friday.

The estimate covers costs through September 3. The Pentagon had obligated about $11.2 billion for military operations and projected another $28.1 billion would be needed to replace expended munitions. A further $4.3 billion was allocated for replacing equipment losses.

The $43.6 billion figure does not include the likely billions of dollars needed to repair US bases and other military facilities in the region damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks, according to Bloomberg.

Iran damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases across eight Middle Eastern countries, according to a Pentagon inspector general report released on Monday. Iranian attacks also damaged or destroyed expensive high-tech radar systems at several US facilities.

The war “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” the report said.

Most of the munitions expenditure stemmed from efforts to intercept Iranian missile and drone strikes, according to an earlier estimate by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). Around 58% of the estimated spending went toward air-defense munitions such as Patriot, THAAD and other key missiles, putting pressure on interceptor stockpiles, the think tank estimated in June.

Washington may have expended more than half of its prewar inventory of Patriot, SM-3 and THAAD interceptors during the conflict, CSIS wrote in a May update.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly denied reports of munitions shortages and called reports and leaks about depleted US weapons stocks “treasonous.”

US forces fired 60 to 70 Patriot interceptors and more than a dozen THAAD missiles against an Iranian volley of around 20 ballistic missiles during an attack on a US base in Jordan on September 8, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed officials.

The expenditure was equivalent to what US forces had used during a full week at other points in the conflict, the newspaper reported. Iran adapted its tactics to force US troops to burn through munitions and used warheads that split into multiple projectiles on approach, the WSJ cited its sources as saying. According to Reuters, the strike damaged multiple US military aircraft.
news.summary:
The US war with Iran has cost $43.6 billion so far, with most of the bill tied to replacing expended munitions
