news.title: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill, aiming to choke off funds for Moscow in Ukraine war
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump on Friday signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russian officials and key pillars of its economy that is meant to punish and pressure Moscow for its ongoing war against Ukraine.

The measure was a final legacy item for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., a close ally and friend of the president who had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. In the works for more than a year, the bill passed with large bipartisan margins: 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House.

It's meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

SEE ALSO: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel, saying attacks are causing a shortage

Sen. Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham's sister, said in a statement Friday: "I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day. I know he would be so proud. Lindsey believed this bill, which he worked on for well over a year, would help end the war through squeezing Putin economically and forcing his customers to reevaluate their relationship with Russia."

Darline Graham was appointed to complete her late brother's Senate term.

"If he were here today, he would be jubilant about our bill's passage - and already thinking about the next one," Blumenthal said of Graham after the House passed the legislation Wednesday evening. Blumenthal added, "Putin is a thug who understands only force and strength, which is what we must show clearly and unequivocally."

Despite overwhelming support on Capitol Hill, the legislation faced criticism from a vocal set of Democratic lawmakers who warned that Trump could use his new expanded tariff powers to impose fresh levies in the European Union and elsewhere.

"Why in the world would this Congress or the People's House give this president unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?" House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said as he laid out his opposition to the bill. "I can't do it."

Graham's journey to getting Trump's sign-off on the bill had been full of fits and starts, as the White House had to be convinced that the president would be able to retain sufficient flexibility on sanctions. Eventually, Trump gave a nod to the bill after it included his push for a five-year extension of existing sanctions on Iran.
news.summary: President Donald Trump on Friday signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russian officials and key pillars of its economy. The measure was a final legacy item for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.
news.author: Seung Min Kim

news.title: Protesters form human chain outside Kennedy Center over closure
news.text:
Joining arm in arm, thousands of protesters partially surrounded the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in a demonstration against a decision close the Washington, DC icon for two years.

The protesters gathered as the sun set on Sept. 18, three days after the decision came down from the center's board, which was hand-picked by President Donald Trump. The move followed a federal judge's second ruling that Trump's name could not be added to the building, culminating months of legal dispute as the president contended that the center needed to be renovated, that only he could raise the money for it, and that his administration should be recognized for it.

"Don't lay a finger on JFK's memorial," said Chris Crowley, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which organized Friday's rally.

The protest drew over 6,400 people who "showed up to protect this memorial to John F. Kennedy," said Tara Hoot, a DC-based drag artist who led the programming. Hoot added that "this stands as a memorial to an assassinated president."

Donning anti-Trump gear, the protesters began the demonstration by joining a performer who sang the National Anthem and ended with a crowd rendition of "America the Beautiful." In between, they chanted "take it down" about a tarp that remains blocking the center's name. The name was blocked after Trump's name was added to the building and then ordered taken down by a judge.

Speakers at the demonstration include actress Lynda Carter, known for her role as Wonder Woman and politicians including U.S. Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, U.S. Rep. Jonathan Jackson of Illinois and DC Councilman Robert White, the Democratic nominee for the district's non-voting congressional delegate seat.

"The Kennedy Center will forever be the people's house," Jackson said. "This is not the Melania and Donald J. Trump House."

More: Kennedy Center closure and Trump's overhaul, explained

Earlier on Sept. 18, Trump continued to defend his stance about his name being on the building, saying that the center had "been a dump" and "lost money" for years. He said that he would subsidize the necessary repairs but said that his administration should be recognized.

"I don’t mind doing the job, but if I do the job, I think the Trump administration, including Bobby, but the Trump administration should be recognized," Trump said in the Oval Office while Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert. F. Kennedy Jr. stood behind him. Kennedy is the nephew of the former president memorialized by the center.

Protesters hoped to wrap an unbroken human chain around the Kennedy Center's perimeter, but fenced-off portions prevented them from completing it. The group linked arms and held hands around the building's eastern front side and southern walls.

One member of the crowd, Amniche Guerin of Prince George's County, Maryland, told USA TODAY that she is "definitely there" any time that there is an opportunity to protest the government.

"But definitely something as sacred as the arts, I think we all need to show up for," she added.

Another attendee, DC resident David Weiss, told USA TODAY that he came out because Trump wants to "put his name on a memorial for an assassinated president" and that the president is "holding it hostage."

news.title: Map Shows GOP-Led States Cracking Down on AI as Trump Rallies Behind Tech
news.text: As President Donald Trump pushes to accelerate America's artificial intelligence boom, governors across the country—including Republicans—are imposing new conditions on the data centers needed to power it. The divide is becoming increasingly visible as the November midterm elections approach. Data centers have moved from being largely an economic-development issue to a political one, with residents in communities across the country raising concerns about electricity prices, water use, land, tax breaks and the cost of building infrastructure for massive new facilities. The result is an unusual tension inside the Republican Party. Trump has made rapid AI development a national priority, arguing that the United States must move quickly to maintain its technological advantage over China. But Republican governors in states including Texas, Florida, Nevada and Nebraska have imposed, or moved toward imposing, conditions on data-center development. Nevada became the latest example on Friday. Republican Governor Joe Lombardo announced tighter conditions for data centers seeking state tax abatements, including requirements concerning taxes, energy costs and the impact of projects on water, infrastructure and communities. Lombardo's administration continues to present data centers as an economic opportunity. But the new rules reflect a growing effort among state officials to ensure that residents are not left paying the costs of the AI boom. Polls Find Majority of Voters Oppose Data Centers A September New York Times/Siena poll found that 61 percent of likely voters opposed the construction of data centers to support AI, compared with 34 percent who supported it. Opposition reached 75 percent among Democrats and 47 percent among Republicans, while independents opposed construction by 60 percent to 36 percent. A separate University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found that 65 percent of Americans opposed building an AI data center in their own community. Even Republicans opposed local construction by 52 percent to 18 percent. The concerns are often less about artificial intelligence itself than about what the infrastructure required to run it means locally. Data centers can consume enormous quantities of electricity. Depending on their design and location, they can also require substantial water resources. Communities are questioning whether utilities, taxpayers and existing ratepayers should bear the cost of connecting facilities to the grid or expanding infrastructure to serve them. That is giving candidates a tangible local issue as they campaign for the 2026 midterms. The New York Times/Siena poll found that AI and data centers remain a relatively low-priority issue when voters are asked what will determine their midterm votes. But the same poll found broad opposition to data-center construction, creating a potentially important distinction between an issue that voters care about in their communities and one they currently rank among their top national voting concerns. The politics therefore do not fall neatly along party lines. Republican voters are broadly more supportive of data centers than Democrats, but recent polling still shows majority Republican opposition to facilities being built in their own communities. For Republican governors, they are left walking a narrow line between following Trump's calls to support AI as an industry while arguing that companies should pay for the electricity, water and infrastructure they consume. What Trump Has Said About AI Trump has repeatedly argued that the United States needs to build AI infrastructure rapidly. In August, he said that if he were a governor or mayor and had the opportunity to bring an AI plant or data center to his community, he would "absolutely want it because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid are just enormous." He has also framed AI as a competition with China. On September 14, while speaking with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a public event, Trump said "whoever wins AI, wins," describing AI as bigger than the internet and saying data centers were an important part of the competition. The same day, Trump rejected calls for additional federal guardrails, describing concerns about AI safety in a Truth Social post as a "HOAX." He said the only control AI needed was "a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT." Trump has nevertheless acknowledged that data-center growth needs to be managed in some respects. He has argued that data centers should produce their own electricity and said communities should benefit economically from the facilities. But his broader message has been that the United States cannot afford to slow AI development while China is competing for technological leadership. Trump's push for AI development has coincided with close working relationships between his administration and major technology companies. The White House has repeatedly brought technology executives into discussions about AI policy and promoted major private-sector investments in AI infrastructure. The administration has also made speeding up permitting and construction a central part of its AI strategy. Trump Wants an AI Boom. Republican Governors Are Adding Conditions Republican governors are confronting a growing tension over the AI data-center boom: They are operating within a party whose president has made rapid AI expansion a national priority, even as certain polls suggest that the majority of Republican voters oppose them. The issue is becoming more politically significant as the November midterms approach, particularly in states where residents are raising concerns about electricity costs, water use and the strain on local infrastructure. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who is up for reelection in November, offers one of the clearest examples of the shift. In November 2025, Abbott joined Google to announce a $40 billion investment in Texas that included new data-center facilities. At the time, he called Texas the “epicenter of AI development” and said, “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” Less than a year later, Abbott ordered a statewide audit of proposed data centers seeking to connect to the Texas power grid. No project can move forward until the review is completed, and projects that fail to meet state requirements can be denied a grid connection. “Our top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life,” Abbott said in announcing the order. “Simply put, Texans must come first.” The governor has since established standards requiring data centers to protect the electric grid, conserve water, account for neighborhood impacts and pay their own way. “They must not pass costs on to Texas families or interfere with their quality of life,” Abbott said. By August, Abbott was also describing the backlash against the industry in unusually blunt terms, telling ABC News that data-center companies had “dug their own grave” by failing to build support in local communities and had gotten “the backlash they deserve.” Trump, meanwhile, had called Texas' opposition to data centers a “mistake.” Other governors have increasingly focused on putting conditions around the industry's physical expansion. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has taken a similar approach. When signing legislation imposing new requirements on hyperscale data centers, DeSantis said the law provided “much-needed protections for taxpayers and our natural resources.” Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen has likewise distinguished between supporting AI and subsidizing the infrastructure required to run it. “I fully support the need for computational services that enable us to stay ahead in the race for artificial intelligence,” Pillen said in a statement. “However, we cannot foot the bill for them.” Pillen said data-center companies are “well-positioned to pay their own way” and argued that Nebraska should not accept projects that deplete its land, water and electricity resources. Nevada's Lombardo has now moved to tighten tax abatements for new data centers while continuing to argue that the industry represents a major economic opportunity for the state. His September 18 executive order reduces the sales-tax benefits available to new facilities and requires companies seeking abatements to make commitments covering their own water and power costs. A Bipartisan Issue Polling found Democrat voters were more strongly opposed to AI and data centers, but for political leaders, the approach is somewhat different. Democratic officials have generally placed greater emphasis on AI safety, transparency and accountability, while some have also moved to address the environmental and infrastructure consequences of data-center construction. California provides the clearest example. Governor Gavin Newsom on Friday issued an executive order accelerating independent oversight of frontier AI companies and directing officials to explore additional safeguards, including a potential emergency "kill switch" for advanced AI models. The order calls for independent verification of AI companies' safety frameworks, transparency reports and risk assessments, while directing officials to develop recommendations for stronger oversight. "We're not waiting to act – we're going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late," Newsom said in a statement. "We're going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action." California is primarily targeting the risks associated with AI systems themselves: safety, transparency, independent audits, privacy, deepfakes and the use of AI involving children and government. Other Democratic-led states have taken action on data centers, too. Pennsylvania has imposed requirements concerning energy affordability, environmental protection, transparency and community engagement for data-center projects seeking state support. New York has pursued restrictions on large-scale data-center development. Oregon has scrutinized the electricity and infrastructure implications of data centers, while Virginia has moved toward greater accountability and transparency for large facilities. The approaches vary, but the underlying question is similar: How should states balance the economic benefits of AI with the associated costs of its expansion? news.summary: Governors across the country—including Republicans—are imposing new conditions on the data centers needed to power AI.

news.title: Germany should profit from Ukraine aid – Merz ally
news.text:
Germany should demand greater economic benefits from the billions it spends supporting Ukraine, including more arms orders and access to raw materials, Bavarian Minister-President Markus Soeder said on Friday.

Since beginning his second term, US President Donald Trump has pushed European NATO members to shoulder more of the cost of supporting Kiev. He has also touted European-funded purchases of US weapons and Washington’s minerals deal with Ukraine as ways for the US to recoup some of its spending on the conflict.

“Overall, Ukraine should also use the many German aid funds to buy more technology from Germany,” said Soeder, who leads the Bavarian CSU, the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU. “And we too, not just the US, should also discuss access to raw materials with Ukraine.”

Rare earths and other critical minerals covered by Washington’s deal with Kiev are used in a wide range of military and high-tech applications.

Soeder’s view echoes recent comments by German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who has argued that Berlin’s support for Kiev should translate into more orders for German arms manufacturers. Germany has earmarked around €11.5 billion ($13.2 billion) in military aid for Ukraine this year.

“It must naturally be the case that the German defense industry benefits,” Wadephul said in a podcast last week.

The push for more Ukrainian arms orders comes as Germany sharply expands its own military procurement. Berlin ordered around €85 billion ($97.4 billion) worth of military equipment in 2025, dominating European arms procurement, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.

Moscow has portrayed Germany’s military buildup, along with broader rearmament across the EU and UK, as evidence that Western governments are preparing for a possible direct confrontation with Russia. It has long described the Ukraine conflict as a NATO proxy war against Russia.

“The statements Merz made about making Germany the leading military power in Europe again are being put into practice. He is, in effect, setting out to declare war on us,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said earlier this month.
news.summary:
Ukraine aid should buy more German arms and provide access to its rare earth minerals, Bavarian premier Markus Soeder has said

news.title: US makes deal to bolster military presence in Greenland while leaving island under Denmark control
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) – President Donald Trump announced on Friday he has a deal with Denmark to bolster the United States military presence in Greenland after months of threatening to take the island by force from the NATO ally – an agreement that also keeps the Arctic territory in Denmark's hands. 

Trump, in a social media post announcing the deal, said the emerging agreement "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns."

He added that with the agreement his administration would "immediately" begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory.

The deal came after officials from US, Greenland and Denmark quietly negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump's security concerns about a territory of roughly 56,000 residents.

For Trump, the Greenland issue had largely been put on the back burner as he launched a military operation to oust former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from power and joined with Israel to start a war against Iran.

With the announcement of the pact, Trump is able to tout a foreign policy achievement ahead of the midterm elections. The six-month-old Iran conflict has reshaped the race, undermining Trump's campaign pledge to steer clear of foreign conflicts and challenging Republicans as they cling to narrow majorities in Congress.

The office of Denmark's prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said the deal will be signed by all three governments next week during the United Nations General Assembly, but parliamentary action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.

In a statement she said, "the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity" of Greenland and Denmark and upholds both people's right "to self-determination".

Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the emerging deal benefits all three governments and "recognizes Greenland's interests".

 ALLIES PUSHED BACK ON TRUMP'S CALL FOR THE US TO ACQUIRE GREENLAND 

With his return to the White House last year, Trump called on Denmark to sell the island to the United States, while insisting Greenland is crucial for US security. He pointedly wouldn't rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the US.

Denmark and Greenland repeatedly said the island is not for sale and condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. The US push for Greenland was also fiercely opposed by Russia and much of Europe.

But Trump, with the announcement on Friday, suggested an understanding may have been reached that could bring an end to what was viewed as an existential crisis by Denmark. 

"We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land," Trump said in his post. "We will be very protective of it!"

Trump had claimed the US needs Greenland to deter threats from Russia and China, and has repeatedly made false claims of Chinese and Russian military forces lurking off the island's coastline.

The agreement bans any non-NATO base in Greenland, limits adversaries from being able to make investments in Greenland and guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, according to a State Department official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio cheered the statement as a "historic deal" and "huge win" for the United States.

"Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area," Rubio said. "This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland."

 THE ISLAND IS CRUCIAL TO NORTH AMERICA'S DEFENSE 

But the US has long had a military presence in Greenland, holding several bases and installations through the Cold War before dialing back its presence.

The US still operates the remote Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which was built after the US and Denmark signed the Defense of Greenland Treaty in 1951. It supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the US and NATO.

Greenland sits off the northeastern coast of Canada, with more than two-thirds of its territory lying within the Arctic Circle. That has made it crucial to the defense of North America since World War II, when the US occupied Greenland to ensure it didn't fall into the hands of Nazi Germany and to protect vital North Atlantic shipping lanes.

Despite Trump's repeated aggressive comments toward Denmark about Greenland, Danish officials had repeatedly made clear that they stood ready to work with the US to expand the American military presence and strengthen US commercial interests in Greenland.

Still, Trump's repeated demands for Greenland and threats to take it by force rattled the NATO alliance and discomfited European allies, said Imran Bayoumi, an associate director at the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.

"I think Americans really underestimate how damaging it was for the image of the United States in Europe," he said. "I think Greenlanders, Danes, Europeans saw this as a real attack on their sovereignty, and it's going to take a lot of work to repair."

news.text:
NEW YORK, September 19. /TASS/. Denmark agreed to a deal with Washington on Greenland because Copenhagen cannot guarantee the island's security, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Friday.

"Denmark and Greenland understand that they don't have the financial means necessary to defend Greenland if it were to come under attack or be threatened. The United States has the power to do that," Rubio told Fox News.

news.title: Guy Named ‘Quantrivious’ And 11 Co-Conspirators Busted For $250,000 Chicken Heist
news.text:
A crew of criminals got caught red-handed hauling a quarter-million dollars in stolen chicken out of a big rig behind a roadside motel.

Federal agents rounded up the group in Memphis, according to a release from the U.S. Marshals Service. A task force made the arrests Tuesday while serving an aggravated robbery warrant on 33-year-old Javunte Johnson. 

Officers found Johnson and a dozen others pulling pallets of poultry, worth $250,000, off an 18-wheeler parked behind a motel, WMC Action News 5 reported. The group scattered, but agents chased down every one of them. (RELATED: Pizza Parlor Owner Says Memphis Is Safer Without National Guard, Refuses To Serve Them)

What started as a warrant sweep turned up far more than frozen birds. Detectives seized three handguns, roughly $110,000 in other stolen goods, and a stash of fentanyl and cocaine, WMC reported. Investigators concluded the merchandise coming off the truck had all been stolen. 

Memphis Safe Task Force Arrests 13 People Trying to Steal $250K Worth of Chicken from a Semi-Trailer#USMarshals https://t.co/Bpp4qhjbW8— U.S. Marshals Service (@USMarshalsHQ) September 17, 2026

Among those hauled in was 25-year-old Quantrivious Shavers, who now faces a theft count, a felon-in-possession charge, and a fentanyl distribution charge, according to Memphis police cited by WMC. Jessie Moore, 37, also caught a felon-in-possession charge. Johnson drew the heaviest slate, including the aggravated robbery count that launched the operation.

Police charged 12 people in the bust. The theft counts, covering property valued between $60,000 and $250,000, landed on Johnson, Shavers, Robert Wilson, 56, Samuel Jackson, 38, John Shipp, 47, Rico Jackson, 36, Devean Hoyle, 45, Trashawn Featherson, 35, Robert Dishmon, 40, and Marcellous McKinney, 38. Wilson and McKinney also caught evading arrest counts, while Moore and 21-year-old Alexis Pike were charged with fleeing on foot. Jackson faces a cocaine distribution count.

The chicken caper was part of a busy day for the task force, which logged 49 arrests total that Tuesday, the Marshals said. President Donald Trump created the multi-agency unit through a memorandum signed in Sept. 2025. The unit pulls in federal, state and local officers alongside Tennessee National Guard members.

Marshals say the operation has produced 12,796 arrests and seized 2,163 illegal guns since it began.

news.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy reaches out to eastern Europe for new trade and security partnership
news.text:
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy launched on Friday a ⁠new trade and security scheme with a group of eight countries from the Carpathian region of central and eastern Europe. In a comment summing up the outcome of the meeting, Zelenskyy said on ⁠Telegram that 50 agreements had been signed for a total value of ​more than €1bn ($1.15bn). ‌He gave few details, but ‌said more than half the accords dealt with energy, particularly solar and ‌wind power, with the aim of energy independence from Russia. The group includes Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary, and the European Union.

At the meeting in western Ukraine, Zelenskyy thanked regional allies for keeping trade and transport ⁠links open following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Polish ‌prime minister Donald Tusk, Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic and Romania’s President Nicusor Dan attended the inaugural event, which is expected ​to last until Sunday. “This marks the start of a movement that should bring our countries even closer together and create another strong framework for cooperation at the EU level,” Zelenskyy said.

Donald Trump on Friday signed legislation enabling sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it to end its war with Ukraine, and also giving him the power to impose additional tariffs on countries breaking the embargo. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, named after the hawkish Republican senator, Lindsey Graham, who died in July, aims to deplete Russia’s ability to continue funding the war by targeting its natural gas and oil revenues, as well as countries that continue to buy Russian energy. The legislation imposes new sanctions on Russian political and military officials and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions.

Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma against a backdrop of intensifying conflict between Russia and Ukraine. There is little doubt that Vladimir Putin’s United Russia will extend its grip on parliament thanks to a tightly controlled vote. The three-day vote began Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday. It is the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that Ukraine was deliberately hindering talks aimed at ending the war and accused Kyiv ⁠of interfering in Russia’s parliamentary ⁠election. Putin, in comments ​to Russia’s Military-Industrial commission, also reasserted Moscow’s main defence aim of relying on its “nuclear triad” of weapons and said Moscow needed to improve its anti-missile defences. In comments reported by Russian news agencies, Putin said Ukraine had “long degenerated into a dictatorship,” referring to the country not holding a new presidential election ⁠despite the expiry of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s mandate.

Latvia’s president has warned that Europe is not keeping up with developments of drone and aerial warfare in Ukraine and that most countries in Nato could not repulse an attack by Russian missiles if the conflict expands. The remarks came during a Guardian interview in Washington DC in which Edgars Rinkēvičs said that the technological developments in drone warfare in Ukraine were moving at “lightning speed”. “What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” he said. “Because if Russia decides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added.

A Russian ⁠glide bomb hit an apartment building in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Friday, killing two people and injuring ⁠seven, leaving three of them ⁠in ​a serious condition. Writing on the Telegram messaging app, President Zelenskyy said ⁠emergency crews had rescued four people after the attack and said others could still be trapped under rubble. The head of Sumy city council said the two dead were city employees. Regional Governor Oleh Hryhorov said three of the seven injured were in a serious condition. Among the injured was a 13-year-old girl.

news.title: Trump, Melania to host Xi and Peng for White House ‘double date’: full schedule
news.text:
Donald Trump and Melania Trump will host Xi Jinping and Peng Liyuan together across two days in Washington next week: a White House welcome, a state dinner at which both presidents speak, a private tea, and a tour of the United States’ founding documents.
Senior US officials set out the programme late Friday and said the pageantry will sit beside talks on artificial intelligence, a trade truce that expires in November, rare earths, fentanyl and detained foreigners.
The briefing confirmed much of what the South China Morning Post had already reported: that AI would be folded into the pre-summit economic talks, that the Busan trade truce and tariff talks were central, and that the visit would be built as a full state occasion rather than a single day of meetings.
Officials described a state visit built around the two couples: a diplomatic double date, with the hard bargaining underneath.
The two couples
On Thursday, 24 September, the Trumps will welcome Xi and Peng to the White House for an arrival ceremony on the State Floor, followed by a military review in the Rose Garden. The two presidents will then hold bilateral talks. Peng Liyuan will leave that track for a separate programme with Melania Trump. The Office of the First Lady may release further details.
That evening the Trumps will host a state dinner for the Chinese delegation in the East Room. Both presidents will speak at the start of the dinner. American guests named by officials include Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Jane Fraser and Tim Cook.
“It’ll be a very popular and hot-ticket event here in Washington, DC,” a senior official said.
Friday, 25 September, is the quieter half. Officials said the Trumps will host Xi and Peng for a private tea at the White House, then the two couples will tour the National Archives, where the United States keeps its founding charters, as the country marks 250 years of independence. Xi will then depart from Washington.
The SCMP reported on 17 September that Trump would greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews, not only at the White House, a rare presidential airport welcome. Friday’s briefing did not dwell on that arrival.
What the leaders are expected to bargain over
The policy list matches the ground the SCMP has been reporting for weeks.
Senior officials said artificial intelligence and the current US-China trade arrangement, the so-called “Busan truce”, struck in South Korea in October 2025 and due to lapse in November 2026, are both on the agenda.
“Those are both on the agenda, both AI and the current quote-unquote Busan truce, and we’ll know more once the two leaders meet,” a senior official said.
SCMP reported on 12 September that Washington and Beijing were discussing folding a long-delayed AI dialogue into the broader economic meeting before the summit, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent handling both files in one sitting.
Bessent is in New York this weekend for high-level talks with Chinese counterparts to prepare the leaders’ meeting.
“Secretary [Bessent] has mentioned that we’ll be up in New York this weekend, talking about this with the Chinese at a very high level at his level,” a senior official said. “I don’t want to get ahead of any conclusions or agreements or non-agreements that may occur over the next couple of days.”
On the rest of the economic file, officials set out several markers.
Washington will not trade additional export control relief for rare earth supplies that officials say were already negotiated. “China’s performance in that respect has not been up to par of what we would expect, and that I’m sure will be a topic of discussion.”
The two sides have discussed cutting tariffs on a “narrow band” of goods that are not strategic and not sensitive.
On any opening of the US car market to Chinese firms, Trump is “not interested in compromising on our national security”.
news.summary:
Donald Trump and Melania Trump will host Xi Jinping and Peng Liyuan together across two days in Washington next week: a White House welcome, a state dinner at which both presidents speak, a private tea, and a tour of the United States’ founding documents.
Senior US officials set out the programme late Friday and said the pageantry will sit beside talks on artificial intelligence, a trade truce that expires in November, rare earths, fentanyl and detained foreigners.

news.title: US weighs delaying Taiwan arms sales until after Apec and G20 summits
news.text:
The United States is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, multiple sources told the South China Morning Post. The potential delay comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to Washington next week for a state visit.
The sources said there was a strong possibility US President Donald Trump could extend the delay through to the end of the year, pointing to a planned bilateral meeting between the two leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and Xi’s expected visit to Florida for the Group of 20 (G20) summit in December.
One source said Trump was considering various options to postpone the signing of Taiwan arms sales, but the final outcome would be a “compromise between him, the China hawks and Taiwan’s lobbyists”.
“President Trump has considered delaying the [Taiwan] arms sales decision till end 2028 or January 2029, that is, towards the end of his current term. However, he faced very loud opposition from hawks after floating the idea,” he said.
“Delaying it after Apec and G20 seems to be the decision for now. There is also a high chance that he will continue to sit on it next year, as Beijing has signalled very strongly against the military sales to Taiwan,” he said.
Noting the existing delivery backlog for Taiwan, the source said a postponed approval “might have limited impact on the actual delivery timeline”.
Taiwan’s orders remain stuck in a long manufacturing queue as American defence contractors prioritise urgent US military inventory replenishment and active combat theatres, especially in the Middle East.
Chronic constraints within the US defence industry – amplified by supply chain bottlenecks and skilled labour shortages – have contributed to the backlog.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.
Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

According to a source familiar with Chinese planning, officials have privately pressed the US to hold off on any new arms sales to Taipei before Xi’s trip to Washington, echoing the message they sent ahead of Trump’s Beijing visit in May.
While Beijing would want sales pushed back as long as possible, officials recognised that Washington could not stall forever, he said.
Meanwhile, Taiwanese officials had voiced concerns about the possibility of Trump delaying arms sales until the end of his presidency, he added.
Two other people familiar with the discussions said the Trump administration could announce a smaller arms package in the window between next week’s Washington summit and the Apec meeting in November, but emphasised that a multibillion-dollar deal like those seen in past years was less likely to materialise.
They said Trump had been advised by some China hawks to take a “piecemeal approach”, approving a small sale first to pacify Taipei. The Trump administration may give Beijing advance notice of any smaller sales to ensure it is not caught off guard and does not view the move as a breach of their understanding, according to sources.
While the Chinese side will certainly oppose a small arms package and publicly express its displeasure, Beijing may reluctantly come to accept it without major retaliation, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Another source described the delay as unsurprising, noting there had been similar delays in the past.
Days before Trump’s May visit to China, his administration put on hold a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan that had been approved by the US Congress.
The package included advanced air and missile defence systems, including PAC-3 Patriot interceptors and the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, or Nasams.
Six months earlier, Washington had announced a separate US$11 billion arms sale to Taiwan, drawing a strong reaction from Beijing.
The current US arms sales delay is not without precedent. Former US president Barack Obama froze arms sales to Taiwan from 2011 to 2015, and George W. Bush did the same from 2007 to 2008.
A source pointed out that Sino-American military ties and the resumption of security dialogue hinged on Washington’s assurances regarding Taiwan.
The SCMP reported on Thursday that the two sides were discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington.
Sources said both Beijing and Washington were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship.
Another potential deliverable under discussion is the resumption of arms-control talks suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan. The dialogue could potentially include military personnel.

news.title: U.S., Denmark reach security deal on Greenland
news.text:
Sept. 18 (UPI) -- President Donald Trump on Friday said the United States reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland for "permanent control over security" of the island.

U.S. and Danish officials said they expect to sign the agreement at the United Nations General Assembly next week.

"At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump said in a statement on Truth Social.

"Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

Trump has expressed his desire to annex Greenland for years, claiming the United States needs it "for defense."

The president said the agreement announced Friday is "completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns."

The United States already has a military presence in the island and an agreement that allows for the expansion of its bases there.

"It is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance," said Jens-Frederik Nielsen, chairman of Greenland's government, in a statement.

"The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all."

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she is "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States."

"An agreement that strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area and is therefore also good for NATO and Europe," the prime minister added in a statement.

"And an agreement that at the same time recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."
news.summary: President Donald Trump said the United States reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland for "permanent control over security" of the island.

news.title: Cuba hit with another blackout as millions across the island are left without electricity
news.text: HAVANA: Cuba’s power grid collapsed once again on Friday, leaving millions of people across the island without electricity for at least the sixth time since U.S. President Donald Trump cut off fuel to the island in January.The Ministry of Energy and Mines announced the islandwide power outage on its official X account and added that officials had begun “activating service-restoration protocols.”“No one can stand these constant blackouts. There isn’t enough food, there’s no water, there’s no electricity -- you have no idea,” Mercedes Rodriguez, a 60-year-old worker in Havana, told The Associated Press as she waited for public transportation to return home. “The country is in such a sad state, and there are no words for what we’re going through.”According to Cuban authorities, a failure reportedly occurred in transmission lines in the western part of the country, causing the system to collapse in that area — as far as Matanzas province — and the eastern section of the island was subsequently disconnected.The official newspaper Granma reported that “unstable” weather conditions further aggravated the grid’s situation.By dusk, power had been restored to 5% of users in Havana, which has a total of about 862,000 customers, according to official data. Small power-distribution “micro-islands” were being established in the provinces of Camagüey, Pinar del Río and Granma. Some systems serving hospitals and other emergency facilities were being reactivated.Power grid collapses have become increasingly common over the past two years because of the severe economic crisis gripping the island. They have worsened since January, after the United States imposed an energy blockade aimed at forcing a change in Cuba’s political system..The restrictions prevent Cuba from importing the fuel needed to operate its thermoelectric power plants, as well as replacement parts required to maintain infrastructure that in many cases has become obsolete. Just one tanker of fuel has been delivered since, by a Russian tanker in March.The two most recent nationwide blackouts occurred in early August, following others in July and March, as well as several regional outages.Even when the national power grid is working, Cubans regularly endure outages lasting more than 30 consecutive hours.The blackouts have had a significant impact on the population and, combined with the energy embargo, have led to transportation limitations, reduced work hours and flight cancellations, in addition to serious public health consequences.The power outages also affect basic activities such as cooking, water supply, and internet and telephone service.Abilén Marrero, a homemaker, sat resignedly at the entrance to her building in central Havana on Friday.“Maybe it’ll come back this afternoon or tomorrow—there’s no way to know. news.title: Your Questions About Trump, Putin, and Russia’s Election Interference Answered
news.text:
On Friday morning, I hosted a Reddit AMA, in which participants could ask me anything. But the questions were practically all related to my new book: How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America. The queries were smart, and none were vituperative—which was surprising given that this topic has become so toxic because of Trump’s BS insistence that “Russia, Russia, Russia” is a Deep State “hoax” and “witch hunt” orchestrated to destroy him. Here’s an excerpt of the Reddit conversation. You can learn more about the book at HowRussiaWon.com.

With Russia’s equivalent of midterm elections happening today, tomorrow, and on Sunday, what do you think the level of US interference in Russia’s election is? Also, historically—say, from the 1990s to now, if we take Russia’s interference in the US as 100 percent—where would you put US interference in Russia? Are the methods employed similar? Different?

DC: We know that historically, Russia has long accused the US and the West of intervening in its domestic affairs. And indeed, throughout the Cold War, the US ran covert actions around the world that intervened in elections and operations that helped overturn democratically elected governments (such as in Iran, Guatemala, and Chile).

But I’ve seen no evidence that the US is doing anything like that in recent years in Russia. Of course, there are intelligence operations that target Russia and Putin. But given that Russia is a closed society, without free media, in which dissidence is crushed and critics imprisoned and killed, there’s much less opportunity for the sort of information operations that Russia can target at an open society like the US and European nations.

Are there signs that the war with Ukraine has affected their ability to interfere with our election due to the allocation of resources?DC: After Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, much of the Russian disinformation operations focused on the war.

Two main lines of false narrative were purported corruption (Zelenskyy is using millions of dollars to buy yachts!) and the bogus charge that the US was running bioweapons labs in Ukraine—an allegation that Tucker Carlson, Tulsi Gabbard, and other MAGA/right-wing influencers embraced and amplified (as I detail in my book).

But during the 2024 campaign, Russian intelligence pivoted to direct its disinfo ops toward the US election—to disparage Biden and then Harris and Walz. And in recent days, we have seen one of those disinfo networks—dubbed Matryoshka—which I wrote about in the book, start to target the midterms to disparage Democrats and encourage votes for the GOP.

Do you have specific examples of what these disinformation campaigns looked like, what each of their intents was, and the platforms they used to do so? The book is full of examples. Here’s one: During the 2024 campaign, a Russian disinformation operator—an American fugitive cop living in Moscow named John Mark Dougan—appeared on a show on Rumble, a conservative video platform, hosted by a QAnoner and presented a man (in silhouette with his voice altered) who claimed he had been a Kazakhstan exchange student at the Minnesota high school where Gov. Tim Walz had once taught and coached football.

This anonymous person said Walz had inappropriately touched him. This baseless allegation—it turned out there were no exchange students from Kazakhstan at the time—was then spread across a network of phony websites set up by Dougan that had real-sounding names: The Boston Times, the New York News Daily, the Miami Chronicle, and was soon picked up by American social media users and went viral across assorted social media platforms.

Eventually, Jack Posobiec, a MAGA influencer who gave us the bonkers Pizzagate conspiracy theory and was then working for the Trump campaign, and Candace Owens, another MAGA influencer, amplified this allegation. It’s a good bet that this baseless charge was seen by over 10 million Americans.

Now, how do you stop something like that? Well, social media platforms could do moderating. More importantly, political operatives and influencers could behave more responsibly. I know. Hah! Not in the world of Trump. But we also can try to encourage everyone to be more discerning in what they pass along. Again, hah! This is a problem. Disinfo ops work best when the phony narratives are embraced and transmitted by real people. How to stop that is a challenge.

When Russia interferes using influencers, are the influencers even aware? Or does Russia just pump money into influencers they believe have the talking points that disrupt or push their agenda?

DC: The best disinformation ops produce false narratives that become embraced and spread by authentic accounts—that is, real Americans.

And we have seen numerous cases in which Russian disinfo slipped into US social media is then widely amplified by MAGA influencers and even Republican officeholders. The book is full of examples of this. And there’s the Tenet Media case, in which RT, the Russian state-controlled propaganda outlet, funneled $10 million to MAGA influencers, including Benny Johnson and Tim Pool, who claim they did not know the exorbitant payments they were receiving—far above normal levels—came from Moscow.

But you have to ask: Why was Russia willing to provide millions to these pro-Trump influencers? What does it say about their role in the information ecosystem?Trump lifted restrictions on using US-supplied weapons for long-distance strikes inside Russia proper, including providing targeting assistance. The blockade of Venezuela saw a further crackdown on the shadow fleet, further restricting Russia’s export capacity. The Russia-friendly Assad regime in Syria has collapsed, and the Russian forces stationed there have been forced to flee.

Why exactly do you think Putin is a fan of Trump despite all that?

DC: I think the answer is obvious. Putin’s key goal is to weaken and divide the Western alliance. Trump is single-handedly doing that, dumping on NATO, threatening Canada, and declaring his intention to grab Greenland. He has cut back on assistance to Ukraine and provided Putin plenty of leeway in that war. Remember when Trump said he would end that war in 24 hours? Well, he has barely tried.

And most recently, he has sided with Putin, with his son-in-law declaring Ukraine should give up land to end the war—Putin’s position. And Trump has definitely weakened the US. Look at the recent news about countries pulling out of their investments in the US. Our position throughout the world is weaker. Our economy is weaker. Trump denigrates American democracy, which is a key part of Putin’s message: You cannot rely on democracy; you need autocratic leadership to have a strong nation.

True, not everything Trump has done has been to Putin’s benefit. He attacked an ally of Putin: Iran. But that has created such upheaval and weakened the US military that it has had benefits for Putin, including raising the value of Russia’s oil reserves.

Does Russia want a specific party in power? Or just to sow division and chaos?

DC: It’s pretty clear that when Russia started to mess with US elections in 2015, its aim was to sow discord and impede the Clinton campaign. Putin hated Clinton—especially for criticizing the 2011 Russian parliamentary elections as fraudulent (which they probably were).

But as Trump became the nominee, the Russian operation included in its goals boosting his campaign. The evidence for this is pretty solid, as I explain in the book. That was the finding of the intel community in early 2017. And the Senate Intelligence Committee released a massive bipartisan 966-page report in August 2020—which got little attention—on the Russian attack on the 2016 election that concluded Putin’s aims had included helping Trump.

Who was chair of the committee at the time and signed off on this conclusion? A guy named Marco Rubio. And, as I detail in the book, Russia’s subsequent interventions in the 2020 and 2024 elections were all aimed at harming the Democrats and helping Trump. Though they do like to increase discord and conflict, as well.

Did you get to work with Nick Offerman for the video about your book? 

DC: I did, and it was both a joy and a thrill to work with him as he recorded the narration, particularly because he asked for notes on his reading of the lines and generously considered suggestions from me and our producer.

news.title: India’s Modi caught between much-needed Russian oil and US trade threats
news.text:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is caught in an energy policy bind with no easy exit.
Cutting Russian oil imports to avoid potential new US tariffs could increase fuel prices ahead of key regional elections, or stress government finances. Maintaining such purchases could cripple Indian exports to its largest market.
India, the world’s third-largest oil importer and among the biggest buyers of Russian crude, reacted unusually strongly on Thursday to a US congressional bill that would allow Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries, including India and China, for major purchases of Russian oil.
The sharp response showed how an energy trade that has delivered India billions of dollars in savings since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is now colliding with its broader strategic and commercial interests.

New Delhi said it had warned the United States that the measure could damage bilateral relations and disrupt global energy markets, vowing to keep “ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people” by buying from diversified sources.
But holding firm could further strain ties with Washington after a turbulent year marked by repeated disputes over trade and tariffs under President Donald Trump. A planned trade deal between the two countries has already faced multiple delays.
Two Indian sources said the latest tensions did not mean Delhi would abandon hopes of striking a trade deal with Washington, though they said India might increasingly need to lean on deals elsewhere if additional US tariffs hit exports.
Since last year, India has signed a trade deal with Britain, finalised one with the EU and is looking to conclude talks on another one with Canada by the end of the year.
Delhi is hoping for a breakthrough when Modi travels to the US for the G20 summit in December, where he could meet Trump on the sidelines, according to one of the sources.
The White House and the Indian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
‘Biggest blow yet’
“The US-India relationship has suffered over the last year for a range of reasons, including US tariffs,” said Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council in Washington.
“But this new legislation, which enjoyed strong bipartisan support and takes the most maximalist position possible on punishing India for its Russian oil buys, may be the biggest blow yet.”
If Washington delayed implementing tariffs or applied them only lightly, the damage could be manageable, he said, adding the legislation nevertheless could widen the trust gap in Delhi for a trade deal and make it harder for Indian negotiators to agree to last-minute concessions needed to secure a deal.
“From the perspective of the trade talks, this new legislation couldn’t have come at a worse time,” he said. “The two sides are not far from the finish line, but getting there will require careful diplomacy.”
The bill has already become a political issue in India, with the opposition urging Modi to adopt a tougher stance. Any hike in pump prices would be risky for Modi, whose party faces elections in India’s most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Modi’s home state of Gujarat starting early next year. Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party runs both Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat.

Before Trump, India was courted by the United States for decades as a strategic counterweight to China, but the world’s fifth-largest economy has repeatedly been left reeling over the past year by decisions taken in Washington.
After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, India sharply increased purchases of discounted Russian crude, which now account for more than 40 per cent of India’s overall oil supplies. The stepped-up purchases were partly the reason Trump imposed tariffs of as much as 50 per cent on Indian goods in August 2025, among the steepest levied on any country.
In February, Trump rolled back those duties in exchange for what he said was India’s commitment to halt Russian oil purchases and lower trade barriers.
But Delhi only briefly reduced purchases from Russia early this year. They have since jumped, especially since the supply shock that followed the US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
Delhi has repeatedly resisted pressure to scale back purchases, arguing that its large population and growing economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies. Indian refiners have already secured crude supplies for September and October that include Russian oil, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Indian analysts said the country’s purchases of Russian oil were not financing the Ukraine war, but only helping stabilise global supplies and keeping domestic prices in check.
“Tariffs of up to 100 per cent would punish Indian exporters and American consumers, disrupt trade and give the US president excessive power over major partners,” said Ajay Srivastava, founder of Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Research Initiative and a former trade ministry official.

news.title: US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The United States, Denmark and Greenland have entered into an agreement that will see the US develop a significant military presence on the island, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases there, Donald Trump said on Friday (Sep 18).

In a Truth Social post, the US president wrote that no US enemies would be able to make sensitive investments on the island without the approval of the United States and that the agreement had no expiry date.

“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will forever have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” Trump wrote.

“Additionally, from now on, no US adversary can ever have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”

Earlier on Friday, Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Greenland were closing in on a deal that would result in an increased US military presence, but would stop well short of Trump’s long-held dream of acquiring the island for the United States.

Trump’s Friday announcement suggests he was nonetheless pleased with the outcome of the negotiations, and that he may not revive his territorial claims, at least in the near future. He said, without elaborating, that the US would soon be rolling out a large military presence on the island, which already hosts one Space Force base in its remote northwest.

“This is a dream come true for the United States of America,” Trump wrote.

The Danish prime minister’s office said on Friday that the agreement would strengthen North Atlantic and Arctic security.

Greenland, Denmark and the United States expect to sign a deal next week to strengthen security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Friday.

“I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” she said in a statement, adding that the agreement would be signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The Greenland security deal reached by the US and Denmark guarantees that China and Russia cannot set up bases there, a US State Department official said Friday.

“The agreement explicitly guarantees the United States the complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent, including permanent access, basing, and overflight rights,” a State Department official said on condition of anonymity.

“This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors.”

news.title: Trump throwing away key swing state with his disastrous move: WSJ
news.text:
President Donald Trump's tariff wars are threatening to put a key swing state Republicans are hoping to contest out of reach, the conservative Wall Street Journal editorial board warned on Friday.

In Michigan, Democratic public health official Abdul El-Sayed, an avowed progressive, is taking on Congressman Mike Rogers, and polls show a close race. Trump, however, has given El-Sayed an inadvertent gift with his constant meddling in trade policy, the board argued.

"Businesses that import goods embed the tariffs into their prices, sometimes in stealthy ways," wrote the board. For example, "Cox Automotive this spring found that Mr. Trump’s tariffs drove a 10.4% increase in the average suggested retail price for new cars. Michigan Smart Trade Alliance estimates tariffs have cost the state $26 billion since January 2025, or about $6,419 per household."

Canadian imports make up a huge portion of the tax revenue, the board noted: America's northern neighbor "exports about $40 billion in goods to Michigan every year. Vehicles and parts make up roughly half of that. Because of its significant car manufacturing, Michigan depends heavily on cross-border supply chains with Canada and Mexico. Michiganders understand that."

Trump has zeroed in on Canada in recent months, massively hiking tariffs there and even threatening trade war with Europe if they move forward with a Canadian partnership.

As all of this is going on, a Republican influence in the Upper Peninsula has a dire warning that campaign volunteering for Rogers is dangerously flaccid.

"You almost have to admire the cynicism of Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on trade," said the board. "He is punching Republican Mike Rogers for not pushing back against Mr. Trump’s Canada tariffs and for previously supporting the North American Free Trade Agreement, which phased-out tariffs on, and boosted trade with, Canada. He’s attacking Mr. Rogers as both a protectionist and a free trader." It's ultimately Trump who made that possible, wrote the board: "Republicans could pay a big political price for Mr. Trump’s tariffs in November."

news.title: Trump extends H-1B visa restrictions, including $100k payment mandate, for another year
news.text: US President Donald Trump has extended restrictions on the H-1B nonimmigrant visa programme for another 12 months, keeping in place a $100,000 payment requirement for certain H-1B workers seeking to enter the US.The White House said in a proclamation signed on Friday that the restrictions imposed in September 2025 would be extended until September 21, 2027. The administration said the move was necessary because the conditions that led to the original restrictions “persist”.“On September 19, 2025, Proclamation 10973 (Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) (2025 Proclamation), was issued to address significant abuses of the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program,” the proclamation said.“The restrictions enacted by the 2025 Proclamation have proven to be highly effective but the underlying conditions necessitating the restrictions persist,” it added.Under the extended policy, the entry of H-1B specialty occupation workers covered by the proclamation will remain restricted unless their petitions are accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment. The restriction applies to workers who are outside the US and seek to enter the country after September 21, 2026.There are limited exceptions. The secretary of Homeland Security can exempt an individual, a company's workers or workers in an industry if their hiring is determined to be in the US national interest and not a threat to the country's security or welfare.The Trump administration has argued that the H-1B system has been exploited by some employers, particularly IT staffing and outsourcing firms, to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign labour.The proclamation said the policy had already produced a sharp change in H-1B filings. According to the White House, combined H-1B registrations by the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms fell from 24,946 to 2,055, a 92% decline. news.title: Is Trump's latest White House media ban legal? It could get complicated
news.text:
WASHINGTON – If recent history is the judge, President Donald Trump faces an uncertain legal landscape after his latest attempt to ban certain media outlets from covering him at the White House.

Trump announced in a Sept. 18 social media post that he is banning reporters from three major media outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and Politico – from the White House because he views their coverage as "FAKE NEWS."

Trump later said there wasn't a specific incident or story that prompted him to initiate the ban, which would not preclue the outlets from reporting on the president.

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," he said.

It's not the first time the Trump administration has taken such action against the press.

During his first term, the Trump White House in 2018 pulled the press credentials of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, complaining that he refused to yield the microphone at a press conference. However, a federal judge appointed by Trump later forced the White House to restore the press pass, saying Acosta hadn't been given a proper chance to defend himself.

And in early 2025, the White House blocked the Associated Press from the Oval Office, The White House East Room, and the press pool that sometimes travels with the president. The White House was upset because the AP declined to change its style for describing the gulf bordering the U.S. and Mexico from the "Gulf of Mexico" to the "Gulf of America." Trump had ordered the name change on official maps.

In the AP's case, one federal trial judge appointed by Trump temporarily blocked the ban. But two appeals court judges - also appointed by Trump - on the three-judge panel reversed that decision in a 2-1 ruling. The case is still being litigated.

The past controversial decisions make for an uncertain legal landscape if the latest media outlets decide to take the White House to court for the most recent ban.

A spokesperson for CNN told USA TODAY in a statement that the ban Trump proposes would be an "illegal assault" on the press. The network said it plans to continue its coverage.

"CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting," the statement said. "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government."

Politico, in a statement, said the publication "will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones" and "will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them."

Representatives of MS NOW declined to comment.

What has Trump said about the legality of banning reporters?

Trump dismissed concerns about violating the Constitution, telling reporters that the move is justified "because they’re fake news."

The president suggested he wanted to make a point, regardless of whether the ban withstands a court challenge.

"We'll see," Trump said when asked what makes him think his ban will be upheld in court. "I think it’s good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn’t . . . depends on the judge you get, to be honest with you. I don't think a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day."

“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Trump added. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my, into the people’s house.”

Trump had few details on what the ban means in practical terms ‒ whether it's the revocation of press badges, removal from the White House pool, or blocking reporters from the targeted outlets from entering the White House campus.

“A very simple ban," Trump said. "I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can.”

The president bristled when a reporter asked whether he's trying to intimidate the media from doing its job. "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press," the president said. 

Where does the AP's lawsuit stand?

The AP initially had success in its lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's ban. Washington, D.C. federal trial Judge Judge Trevor McFadden, who was appointed by Trump, ruled the ban probably violated the First Amendment's free speech protections and issued a temporary order blocking it.

"(U)nder the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists - be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere - it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints," McFadden wrote.

However, in a 2-1 decision governed by two other Trump appointees, Judges Neomi Rao and Gregory G. Katsas, an appeals court panel largely struck down McFadden's order. It said blocking the White House from restricting specific reporters' ability to join other reporters in the Oval Office or the press pool interferes with the president's authority.

"While the AP has alleged financial loss from being denied access to the Oval Office, that harm does not, inour view, justify an intrusion on presidential prerogatives during this litigation," Rao wrote, in an opinion joined by Katsas.

Judge Cornelia T.L. Pillard, an appointee of President Barack Obama, dissented, writing that her colleages' view "cannot be squared with . . . any sensible understanding of the role of a free press in our constitutional democracy."

Trump's latest targeted reporter ban appears to go further than the ban on the AP, barring reporters "from the White House," according to his social media post.

That may not hold muster even with the judges who largely ruled with the Trump administration before. Those judges did overturn an attempt by the White House to block the AP from accessing the White House's East Room, noting it is "a much larger space that can accommodate more members of the press." And those judges specifically noted the ban on the AP didn't block it from entering White House press facilities such as the main briefing room.

The AP's case is still under litigation.

What do experts say about the ban?

Clay Calvert, a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, called the bans “thoroughly unsurprising,” particularly as Trump faces low approval ratings heading into the midterms. 

The news media is an “easy target” for Trump, Calvert said, and implementing the ban is likely to appeal to his political base that overwhelmingly distrusts mass media. 

Though it echoes Trump’s earlier ban on the Associated Press, Calvert described that as a “much more precise target” centered on a single decision – the news outlet refusing to adopt “Gulf of America” after Trump renamed the body of water widely known as the “Gulf of Mexico.” The ban was also limited to certain spaces, including Air Force One and the Oval Office. 

It's not immediately clear whether CNN, MSNOW and Politico would face similar restrictions or be barred from the White House entirely.

Barring journalists from the White House or other spaces where the government operates can make it “really difficult” to get information to report to the wider public, ACLU senior policy counsel Jenna Leventoff told USA TODAY. 

A federal judge blocked a press policy the Pentagon implemented in 2025 that said journalists who "solicit" information not approved for public release could lose access to the building. The Pentagon then imposed an interim press policy that required journalists to be escorted through the premises at all times, which was also struck down. 

But the potential to get involved in a costly and time-consuming legal fight with the Trump administration may make some news outlets “think twice” about their reporting, Leventoff said. 

“In that respect, it doesn’t matter if he wins in court or not, because he’s still chilling the media from saying things he dislikes,” she said. 

National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. said in the organization’s news release on the matter that Trump “weakens one of the nation’s strongest checks on those who hold power” by blocking access to his administration. 

He said the latest ban would be an “unprecedented assault on press freedom” if implemented and underscored journalists’ role in informing the American public. 

“A government confident in its actions should never fear independent scrutiny,” he said.

news.title: Trump, Denmark strike deal to expand US military presence in Greenland
news.text:
Washington: Denmark, the United States and Greenland are expected to sign an agreement that will allow the US to increase its military presence in the Danish territory and ban adversaries such as Russia and China from building bases or making sensitive investments there.

The agreement was simultaneously announced by all three parties and will be signed at the United Nations next week when world leaders converge on New York for the UN General Assembly’s high-level meetings.

It is a significant win for US President Donald Trump, who made Arctic security a key plank of his foreign policy agenda, but frightened European allies with his demands for the US to purchase Greenland or perhaps take the Danish territory by force.

Based on details provided by a US State Department official, the deal stops well short of giving the US control over Greenland, but expands American access and puts explicit, permanent restrictions on the presence of NATO adversaries.
